title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
raw_text: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

title: A bridge to modernization: What IDC’s Market Note says about Cameyo by Google

Yet for many IT leaders, business-critical legacy desktop apps stand in the way—too essential to retire, too complex and costly to rewrite—yet unequipped for the security challenges and productivity opportunities of the AI era. That doesn’t have to block your modernization strategy. By delivering Windows and legacy applications directly inside the Chrome browser, Cameyo by Google connects legacy workflows to Chrome Enterprise, ChromeOS, and Gemini—with zero replatforming required. In a recent IDC Market Note, “ Cameyo by Google: A Modern Bridge Technology Platform in Digital Workspace Transformation , ” lead analyst Filippo Vanara examines how Cameyo reduces deployment complexity while enhancing security and lowering costs. Here are five of our key takeaways from the IDC Market Note: Rebuilding legacy apps costs millions: Virtual App Delivery (VAD) is the bridge Enterprise modernization barriers make rewriting or replatforming legacy applications unfeasible for many organizations. The IDC report notes that "Cameyo is positioned as a strategic bridge between legacy application environments and modern, AI-driven digital workspaces." By connecting legacy systems to modern, AI-enhanced digital workspaces, Cameyo enables organizations to safeguard their existing technology investments. 2. With Cameyo, legacy workflows run right alongside built-in enterprise AI like Gemini in Chrome—giving employees safe, managed AI tools instead of pushing them toward unmanaged "shadow AI." At the same time, apps can inherit Chrome’s advanced threat protections and Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies through Chrome Enterprise Premium, which the IDC Market Note highlights "This enables organizations to extend AI capabilities and modern security controls to legacy workflows." 3. Protecting your organizations from cyberattacks Traditional VDI utilizes open VPNs and public server ports that leave organizations vulnerable to cyberattacks. According to the IDC Market Note, "As part of its value proposition, security is central to Cameyo. In fact, the platform adopts a zero trust architecture, isolating users, sessions, and resources from the corporate network.” Additionally, "the use of non-persistent infrastructure and a simplified architecture reduces the overall attack surface." 4. Slashing operational and virtualization costs According to IDC's 2025 EMEA CloudOps Survey (n = 509) findings, 89% of organizations in Europe estimated that they are currently wasting their public cloud spending. When companies use Cameyo as opposed to complex virtual desktops, they consistently realize reduced costs. According to the IDC Market Note, "Cost is another core value proposition for Cameyo as it emphasizes its potential to deliver significant cost savings compared with traditional VDI and DaaS solutions: up to 54% reduction in total cost of ownership (TCO) when transitioning from legacy environments." 5. Phased modernization across endpoints According to the IDC Market Note, IDC believes Cameyo represents an important evolution within the broader VCC market, specifically reflecting a shift from desktop-centric virtualization to application-centric delivery models. In this context, the platform functions as a bridge technology, enabling enterprises to modernize incrementally rather than requiring full application replatforming. This aligns with IDC's view that most organizations will pursue phased modernization strategies, maintaining legacy software while gradually transitioning to cloud-native architectures.” By delivering legacy applications as Progressive Web Apps (PWAs), Cameyo helps businesses modernize without being tethered to a specific device or operating system. When paired with ChromeOS Flex, Cameyo can ensure seamless access to those legacy apps on older devices, extending existing hardware lifespans and reducing capital expenditures. title: Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux
raw_text:
The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load. Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs. To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko , an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year. In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild. Reviewing code is hard Reviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code. To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative: LLMs often struggle to put in enough effort. LLMs are trained to achieve the goal of spending fewer tokens. So they often tend to cut corners and dismiss concerns without proper investigation or flag false positives without proper due diligence. LLMs are easier to bias . The current generation of LLMs usually performs much better if provided a single relatively simple task (e.g., prove the patch for memory leaks) rather than multiple tasks (e.g., explore several complex, varied concerns). It’s pretty common for an LLM to find an obvious issue in the code and refuse to look deeper for other types of issues. Also, commit log text can sometimes affect the result of code review in a non-predicatable or even malicious way. LLMs don’t have persistent memory. Surprisingly, this is a positive thing for code review: An LLM can review the same or similar patch multiple times as if it were a new patch. No sane human can review the same patch applied to 100 slightly different branches to find the few that have incompatible changes. How Sashiko reviews a patch To avoid these failure modes, Sashiko separates finding candidate bugs from verification of those bugs , and requires each pass to record what it ruled out: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Gather context and plan
 -> Parallel specialist sessions (concerns + dismissed concerns)
 -> Triage
 -> Per-bug deep checks
 -> Review report'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f46884251d0>)])]> Notes on each step: Gather context and plan: Sashiko first pulls in the code around the diff (modified functions, struct definitions, and direct callers) and loads the subsystem's domain guides, so the changed lines are never judged in isolation. A planner then decides which specialist passes are needed (skipping hardware checks on pure software code, for example) and sets a reasoning budget for each pass based on patch complexity. Parallel specialist sessions: Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on a single class of problems: commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security, and hardware. Giving each pass a single focus prevents one type of bug from crowding out another. Each session searches and reads the repository with git tools (averaging about 100 tool calls per review) and outputs two lists: concerns it believes are real, and candidate concerns it investigated and ruled out, along with the code that supports that conclusion. Triage: A lead verifier audits those two lists together. Clear-cut bugs already proven by the code in front of it pass straight through; dismissals proven by a local check are dropped. Everything else deserves additional investigation. Crucially, that includes not only contested bugs where specialists disagreed, but also shaky self-dismissals — cases where a specialist spotted a real bug and dismissed it by assuming, without proof, that some unseen caller or lock would prevent it. Per-bug deep checks: Instead of checking all difficult cases in one shared prompt, Sashiko gives each difficult case its own verification agent that runs in parallel. Each agent gets one specific question to answer with git tools under a symmetrical rule: Neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. If a specialist talks itself out of a real bug based on a false assumption, this step catches it and promotes it back to a real finding. Review report: Sashiko generates a report that sounds like a human maintainer asking questions about the proposed change, matching the style expected on a Linux mailing list. All this happens at no cost for developers. Deep agentic reviews at scale require a substantial token budget. If developers had to pay for them with their own API keys, many important contributors would be pushed away. Instead, Sashiko reviews patches sent to public Linux kernel mailing lists, and Google runs the service at sashiko.dev . Everything runs in the open: every prompt, tool call, reasoning step, and ruled-out bug is public. The project initially used the open-source Linux review prompts started by Chris Mason, and more than 100 contributors, including prominent kernel maintainers and engineers, have since helped to improve prompts and Sashiko itself. Recently, Sashiko switched to a different prompt system that combines per-tree or per-version auto-generated notes on code with subjective maintainers notes, which contain directions and instructions from maintainers that can’t be derived from the code. What the data shows The real test of an automated reviewer is whether maintainers pay attention to the reports it sends out, and whether those reports track actual software quality. Seven months of Sashiko production data from the kernel mailing lists give a clear picture of both these questions. It is part of the daily workflow. Sashiko completes roughly 1200 reviews a day across over 100 kernel mailing lists. It sends review emails only to lists whose maintainers opt in, and already over 70 of them have done so. Developers also engage directly with the reports: More than 1500 kernel developers have replied on the mailing lists, and their pushback on false alarms has directly driven improvements to Sashiko's prompts and verification engine. In fact, LWN.net recently wrote that Sashiko has already become an important part of the kernel's development process and was the top bug reporter of issues in the 7.2 release cycle. It prevents new bugs and uncovers old ones. When Sashiko flags a bug in a proposed patch, the author typically fixes it in the next revision before the change is ever merged. Many developers run Sashiko locally or in corporate private instances. The bugs that Sashiko helped to prevent leave no trace in the git commit log, making them hard to count directly. What can be counted are fixes for preexisting bugs that Sashiko finds and reports as a byproduct of reviewing new changes: Sashiko is cited in over 2000 mainline kernel commits and in over 500 of this year's official Linux kernel CVEs, spanning drivers, core kernel code, networking, GPUs, memory management, and virtualization. Fewer bugs are slipping into mainline releases. Across the 18 kernel releases prior to Sashiko (Linux 6.2 through 6.19, covering 254000 commits), an average of 3.4% of merged commits required a follow-up fix within 60 days. Since Sashiko rolled out, that 60-day fix rate has fallen to 2.8% in Linux 7.1 and 2.2% in Linux 7.2, a 35% drop (with the 30-day fix rate falling from 2.3% to 1.4%). It’s too early to make strong claims, and obviously many other factors can influence release-to-release numbers, so we cannot solely credit Sashiko for the entire drop, but the trend is optimistic. Since Sashiko was rolled out, the percentage of merged commits in the Linux kernel that received a follow-up fix in 60 days has dropped by 35%. A clean review carries real signal. If Sashiko's warnings were mostly noise, commits merged with warnings would need follow-up fixes no more often than commits that passed cleanly. In practice, across 21,500 tracked mainline commits, patches that received a clean Sashiko review required a follow-up fix within 60 days just 0.9% of the time — less than a third of the historical baseline. Patches merged despite a critical Sashiko warning needed a fix 7.6% of the time — an 8x higher risk (and 6.3x higher even after adjusting for patch size). That gap is what makes Sashiko useful to maintainers: A clean pass instills real confidence, while a critical warning is a strong reason to take another look at the proposed patch. This all tracks with what Linus Torvalds wrote in a mailing-list discussion a few weeks after Sashiko’s launch: "As you say, Sashiko tends to be quite good. Even when it flags something unnecessarily and there's no actual problem, there's likely to be a reason for the question. And we've seen some truly stellar reports too. Things that are deep and subtle, and the AI is 100% correct. So anybody who thinks that all AI is slop is in denial about the current state." - Linus Torvalds ( on lore.kernel.org ) Sashiko at a glance Since March 2026 Patch reviews completed 241,000 (~1200+ / day) Opted-in kernel subsystem lists 75+ Mainline commits crediting Sashiko 2,000+ 2026 Linux kernel CVEs crediting Sashiko 528 60-day post-merge fix rate Down from 3.4% baseline to 2.2% (Linux 7.2) What we learned from building and running Sashiko First, benchmark-driven development beats intuition. While developing Sashiko, we tried many ideas that looked very reasonable on their face but didn’t end up working out. Other ideas were less obvious but worked surprisingly well. What was crucial: Early on, we built a benchmark out of nearly 1,000 real Linux kernel bugs and used it to evaluate every major Sashiko change. Every bug in this set was a real mistake that had passed human review by kernel experts, had been merged into mainline Linux, and later had to be fixed. On that benchmark, Sashiko with the new Gemini 4 Carbon model catches 75.8% of the bugs that human reviewers missed (using high thinking level). Second, coding agents are not great at reviewing their own code. Models are trained to produce a working solution within a limited token budget. Asking these agents to review their own code might work well for isolated tasks, but for real, large codebases, creating a functional solution is often just 5-10% of the work. What’s really hard is to produce a solution that works all of the time, is well-integrated into the surrounding code, and doesn’t introduce subtle regressions. This is often substantially more complex and requires additional effort. Similar to human developers, agents benefit from external code review: Reviewers often spot issues that the initial author missed, even if they are not more experienced. Third, open source and shared community ownership and development help to build trust. By being fully open and transparent from the beginning , Sashiko allowed anyone to run it the way they wanted: using different models (including open source and local models), customizing prompts, or even adopting Sashiko to other-than-Linux projects. This helped with community adoption and brought over 100 contributors to improve Sashiko, including some prominent kernel developers. More and more engineers are putting local Sashiko instances into their coding-agent loops, so patches are checked against the community's review rules before a human maintainer ever sees them. We use the same workflow to build Sashiko itself ("Sashiko for Sashiko"), running it to review every change to its codebase and prompt pipeline both locally and through a Github integration. Although Sashiko started in the Linux kernel, the need for an agentic trust layer applies across critical open-source software. Because the core review engine does not depend on C or on kernel-specific rules, the Linux kernel playbook (combining an open verification pipeline, community-owned domain guides, and a benchmark mined from historically known issues and fixes) can likely be applied to other foundational open-source projects such as GCC, LLVM, or Git. "Now, I think the other side of AI - and this is where Sashiko comes in - is that it basically does end up being a tool that can then increase the trust in the patch. So AI giveth, and AI taketh away. But the basic issue shouldn't be AI per se, it should be that notion of 'trust'." - Linus Torvalds on LKML You can check out Sashiko at sashiko.dev , or find the code on GitHub to run it in your own development workflow.
summary: The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers.

title: What’s new in OKF v0.3: enterprise-ready knowledge, use cases, and skills
raw_text:
In June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) , an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need. In July, v0.2 added trust signals: provenance, trust, freshness, lifecycle, and attestation. In production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way. Released today, OKF v0.3 adds precise conformance rules, trust tiers that keep pace with agent edits, self-describing bundles with licensing, safe ways to retire and move knowledge, a stable extension model, and a clear versioning policy. However, the core idea behind OKF stays the same: type is still the only required field, and your existing bundles keep working. We're also launching OKF use cases , which are community guides for using OKF alongside other industry standards, and two agent skills that let coding agents write and read OKF bundles. Finally, to make cross-organization collaboration easier, we’re moving OKF out of the Google Cloud Platform GitHub org into a standalone organization at https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/ . Let’s take a closer look at what’s new in OKF v0.3. Built for interoperability v0.3 adds a formal conformance section, allowing independent producers and consumers to work together by design. The spec is self-contained and uses RFC 2119 keywords. It gives one clear answer to the questions that come up when tools from different teams and vendors read the same bundle. The full detail is in the spec, but a few themes matter for anyone building on OKF: Built on standard file formats. OKF uses a small, widely supported set of standards: YAML 1.2 frontmatter, CommonMark with GFM tables and footnotes, and RFC 3339 timestamps. If your tools handle those, they handle OKF. OKF bundles share space with other markdown files. A .md file without a type is skipped by OKF consumers, so README.md , AGENTS.md , CONTRIBUTING.md , and SKILL.md can live inside a bundle without breaking it. Files that aren't markdown, like images or attester code, are assets that concepts can link to. Consumers handle real-world input predictably. Bundles written by many agents can contain nulls, empty strings, single values where a list was expected, and new vocabulary. v0.3 specifies how a consumer reads each of these. Consumers accept these inputs without failing, while validators log warnings for malformed entries. A bundle never fails because an optional field is missing or a link is broken. Trust that keeps pace with agents v0.2 gave every concept a trust tier: unverified , machine-confirmed , or human-reviewed . As agents take on more of the editing, v0.3 makes sure the tier always reflects the latest version of the content. Here's a typical sequence: A person reviews a metric definition and signs off. A week later, an agent refines the definition. The trust tier now reflects that the person hasn't yet reviewed the new text. In v0.3, only current verifications count . A verification is current when it happened at or after the last meaningful change to the content, recorded in generated.at : code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'generated: { by: reference_agent/gemini-2.5-pro, at: "2026-09-02T10:00:00Z" }
verified:
 - { by: "human:jsmith", at: "2026-08-25T09:00:00Z" } # before the rewrite: history
 - { by: "process:finance-nightly", at: "2026-09-03T02:00:00Z" } # current'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f46792e5290>)])]> This concept is now machine-confirmed , not human-reviewed, until a person confirms it again. The older sign-off stays in the file as history, and a UI can show it as "reviewed before the last change." v0.3 also standardizes actor identifiers. Actors are <producer>/<version> for tools, or <scheme>:<id> for everything else, and v0.3 adds team: next to human: and process: . Only human: earns human-reviewed, because a team name doesn't say which person actually checked the content. Bundles that describe themselves When an agent has access to dozens of bundles, bundle-level metadata supports progressive disclosure so it can pick the right bundle without reading every file. In v0.3, the bundle-root index.md can carry frontmatter about the bundle itself: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '---
okf_version: "0.3"
title: Acme retail analytics
description: Tables, metrics, and sanctioned computations for Acme retail. Use it for sales and margin questions.
license: CC-BY-4.0
---'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f467894bf10>)])]> description is written for routing. In one sentence it says what the bundle covers and when to use it. license makes clear what you're allowed to do with knowledge you receive from someone else. okf_version tells a consumer which rules to apply, including compatibility fallbacks for older bundles. Tools that regenerate index.md must keep this frontmatter. A lifecycle with forwarding addresses Knowledge evolves, and an agent that finds a deprecated concept should be able to get to its replacement. v0.3 adds superseded_by : code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'status: deprecated
superseded_by: /metrics/gross-margin.md'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f467894b550>)])]> Consumers that filter to current knowledge follow the pointer and return the replacement. The same mechanism handles moves and renames. Leave a short deprecated concept at the old path that points to the new one, and existing links and stored references keep working. One rule for links and paths Links in the body and path fields in frontmatter ( resource , superseded_by , executor.resource , and others) now resolve the same way: A value with a scheme ( https: ) is an absolute URL. A value that starts with / resolves from the bundle root. Anything else resolves from the directory of the file that contains it, just like on GitHub or in any markdown editor. For bundles marked v0.2 or earlier, or with no version, a consumer can also resolve paths from the bundle root, so existing bundles keep working. v0.3 also makes explicit that links are not parent/child relationships. Only the directory tree defines hierarchy. A link is an untyped, directed relationship, and the text around it says what kind ("joins with," "replaces," "depends on"). Path fields that point at concepts are edges in the bundle graph too. Room to extend, without collisions The community has been extending OKF since v0.1, with typed edges, routing hints, and erasure profiles. v0.3 makes a few extension mechanisms a first-class rule: Extension keys are allowed at any level , including inside sources entries, verified events, executor , and attester . A producer that edits a file must keep the keys it doesn't understand so one tool doesn't overwrite metadata added by another. Future OKF versions will never define keys that start with x- . Name your keys x-<producer>-<name> , for example x-acme-owner , and they won't collide with a future spec version. A versioning policy before 1.0 v0.3 defines OKF's versioning rules. Before 1.0, minor versions may include breaking changes as long as each is documented with a consumer fallback where possible. Starting at 1.0, minor versions will be strictly additive, and released normative text will not change in place. The spec also lists what was considered and deferred : typed relationships, the full attestation runtime protocol (receipt and verdict wire formats), semantic-layer attestation, validity windows, and a refuted verification event. Until the community agrees on a form for these, extension keys are the place to experiment. We'd like your proposals. Introducing OKF use cases OKF keeps its core specification small and links to existing domain schemas like Avro, Protobuf, or OpenAPI instead of duplicating them. In practice, though, when your organization already has an established artifact in another standard, such as a schema, a contract, or a spec, what should the OKF concept next to it say, and how should an agent use the two together? Starting with v0.3, we're publishing use cases : guides for using OKF with other industry standards. Each one explains: Where the boundary sits : what belongs in the other standard and what belongs in OKF. How to link the two : which frontmatter and link conventions point from a concept into the other artifact. What an agent should do with the combination. A complete worked example you can copy. Use cases are layered on the core spec, not part of it. A bundle that ignores them is still a conformant OKF bundle. When a convention proves itself across several use cases, it can be proposed for the core spec through the usual process. Use cases are managed directly in GitHub. Each use case gets its own folder under usecases/ in the OKF repository, for example usecases/<usecase>/ . The guide is a .md file in that folder, and any sample bundles or artifacts sit next to it. Use cases are reviewed, versioned, and discussed like any other change. Propose a use case If you pair OKF with a standard, please send us a proposal. A rough first draft is welcome. Open a pull request that adds a folder under usecases/ with a .md file in it, and we'll refine it together in review. Compatibility v0.3 has two breaking changes, and existing v0.2 bundles stay readable: Path fields resolve relative to their file. Fallback: for bundles marked v0.2 or earlier, or with no version, consumers can resolve from the bundle root. Only current verifications count toward the trust tier. No fallback needed, since tiers can only go down. Everything else is a clarification or an optional addition. v0.1 fallbacks ( timestamp , body # Citations ) still apply. Agent skills for OKF The two skills live in the new repository and follow the open Agent Skills format, so any agent that supports skills can load them. okf-generate writes, updates, migrates, and validates bundles from available sources. It cites a source for each claim, records a human review only when that person confirms it, and copies attested computations from a sanctioned source instead of writing them. okf-consume answers questions from a bundle. For each concept used, it reports the trust tier, status, freshness, and attestation result, and runs attested computations only through the bundle's configured executor and attester. To install them in Gemini CLI, run: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# install okf-generate
gemini skills install https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format --path skills/okf-generate

# install okf-generate
gemini skills install https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format --path skills/okf-consume'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f4678949dd0>)])]> The README lists the install steps for other agents. Get involved Read the v0.3 spec . Add okf_version to your bundles, and check that your consumer computes trust tiers from current verifications only. Issues and pull requests, including new use case proposals, are welcome on GitHub. Spec, samples, use cases, and reference implementations: https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/
summary: In June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) , an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need. In July, v0.2 added trust signals: provenance, trust, freshness, lifecycle, and attestation. In production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way. Released today, OKF v0.3 adds precise conformance rules, trust tiers that keep pace with agent edits, self-describing bundles with licensing, safe ways to retire and move knowledge, a stable extension model, and a clear versioning policy.

title: Building an agentic stack in Envoy: routing models, tokens, and MCP
raw_text: At Google Cloud, we believe the next generation of AI and agentic systems must be built on open, battle-tested foundations. Envoy, an open-source edge and service proxy designed for cloud-native applications, has already transformed microservices and modern cloud networking, powering everything from Google Cloud’s Application Load Balancers to the Agent Substrate dataplane on Google Kubernetes Engine. Now, Envoy is uniquely positioned to become the open standard for AI traffic, MCP tooling, and agent-to-agent communication. Earlier this year, we presented the technical case for Envoy networking in the agentic AI era , examining how autonomous AI agents fundamentally challenge traditional Layer 7 networking assumptions. Unlike microservices, autonomous agent workloads choose who they communicate with. In addition, their routing attributes live deep within request bodies, with their traffic governed by token budgets as well as request rates, and their multi-turn reasoning loops requiring stateful session affinity and strict tool execution boundaries. At Google Cloud, we have been working hard to develop Envoy for the agentic era. Read on for a closer look at how Envoy has evolved to better support autonomous agents, giving developers the performance and portability of an open-source ecosystem, backed by enterprise security and scalability. Why autonomous agents challenge traditional L7 proxies Over the past decade, Envoy became the industry standard for cloud-native traffic management by operating cleanly at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP connection management) and Layer 7 (URI, method, and header-based routing). Autonomous agents introduce two higher-order protocol layers: Layer 8 (agentic interaction protocols): such as LLM APIs , Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A) , running over JSON-RPC 2.0 or gRPC. Critical policy attributes—such as tools/call , tool_name: "execute_sql" , or model: "gemini-1.5-pro" —are serialized inside the request payload. Layer 9 (agent framework interfaces): Coordination frameworks such as UCP, AP2, and Google Cloud’s Agent Development Kit, where multi-turn workflows produce dynamic token consumption and non-linear execution graphs. Fronting these workloads with traditional L7 proxies creates four major architectural challenges: Payload blindness: Nearly all LLM traffic shares the same paths (such as /v1/chat/completions ), so a header-based proxy cannot distinguish between a low-cost query and an expensive 500,000-token prompt, or one model from another. Request rate limiting fallacy: One request per minute with a massive context window can use more accelerator compute and memory bandwidth than dozens of short queries, and agent loops can burn through budgets unnoticed. Stateless load balancing: Each turn of an agent's conversation should go back to the server that already remembers it. Traditional load balancers send it to whichever server is next, so the model has to start over for every turn, this wastes time and GPUs. Ungoverned tool execution: Agents query databases, execute code in sandboxes, and call third-party APIs. Without inline inspection of MCP tool calls, organizations risk prompt injection, data exfiltration, and runaway billing loops. The core pillars of Envoy’s agentic stack To address these challenges, Envoy provides capabilities that turn the network into an active governance layer: Core Pillar Operational Functionality 1. Native body parser Payload blindness: Read request bodies, not just headers. Line-rate payload normalization across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini schemas with SSE stream handling. 2. Tokenomics engine Request-rate fallacy: Count tokens, not just requests. Pre-inference token estimation, tokens per minute (TPM) / tokens per day (TPD) rate limiting 3. Model & MCP routing Stateless load balancing: Keep agent sessions on the right servers Endpoint Picker (EPP) model dispatch, KV-cache prefix affinity, MCP Stateless support. 4. AI security guardrails Ungoverned tool execution: Policy tool calls. Inline policy, decision point (ext_proc) callouts for guardrails: Model Armor, ShieldGemma, and data loss prevention. 1. Native wire-format body parsing and transcoding Client applications often get locked into specific model APIs. For example, client code built for OpenAI's schema cannot communicate with Anthropic's endpoints or Google’s Gemini without client-side translation layers. To help, Envoy ecosystem includes native body parsers that normalize requests across diverse model families, providing: Client abstraction: Upstream applications send a standardized schema. Envoy inspects the JSON payload at line-rate, extracts the target model, and dynamically transcodes the request into the downstream provider's native format. No application code changes: Switching from an external commercial model to a self-hosted open-source model (such as Gemma or Llama on vLLM) requires only an Envoy configuration update. Application code remains unchanged. Streaming token extraction: Envoy parses server-sent events (SSE) response streams in real time, capturing token counts from usage chunks while maintaining ultra-low time-to-first-token latency. 2. Tokenomics engine: token-aware traffic management In AI networking, tokens are the fundamental unit of capacity . Envoy replaces coarse request counters with token-aware traffic management features such as: Token rate limiting: Enforces tokens per minute (TPM) and tokens per day (TPD) limits per tenant, project, or model. Pre-inference throttling: Envoy estimates input tokens from request payload bytes and extracts actual token usage from LLM responses to record in a quota database, rejecting subsequent over-quota requests with an HTTP 429 before they reach the inference cluster. Runaway loop protection: Autonomous agents can enter recursive reasoning loops. By tracking cumulative token consumption and message counts per session or agent ID, Envoy throttles multi-turn sessions once an agent exceeds its assigned budget. 3. Model routing and Model Context Protocol (MCP) support Envoy manages traffic for both downstream model backends and outbound tool calls, with: KV-cache prefix affinity: Using the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extensions and Endpoint Picker (EPP), Envoy routes prompts sharing identical system instructions to the GPU worker currently holding that cache in memory, reducing latency. Model retry and fallback: If a primary model returns a 429 status code or fails, Envoy automatically retries or redirects the request to a secondary model pool with zero client interruption. MCP tool routing: For MCP agents, Envoy routes requests via JSON-RPC 2.0 bodies and HTTP headers. Per the 2026-07-28 MCP specification , Envoy uses Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers for zero-body-parsing routing to backend servers. Backends reject header-body mismatches with an HTTP 400 / -32020 (HeaderMismatch) error to prevent tampering. 4. AI security guardrails Inline safety filtering cannot come at the expense of network throughput. To prevent this, Envoy provides security callouts: Using standardized external processing ( ext_proc ), Envoy connects to dedicated policy decision engines — such as Google Cloud’s Model Armor, ShieldGemma, or local classifiers — to detect prompt injections and sensitive data leaks with minimal latency overhead. High-density infrastructure: Envoy and Agent Substrate In enterprise production environments, agents frequently spend time idle between user queries or long-running tool executions. Running hundreds of thousands of idle agents in dedicated containers or virtual machines can create prohibitive infrastructure costs. Envoy pairs directly with high-density execution runtimes like Agent Substrate to provide: Scale-to-zero traffic steering: Agent Substrate uses lightweight isolation runtimes (such as Cloud Hypervisor, microVMs and gVisor application sandboxes) that can suspend and resume in milliseconds. When traffic arrives for a suspended agent, Envoy buffers the initial packet while signaling the runtime to resume the instance, completing the end-to-end resume in milliseconds. Egress perimeter defense: Envoy functions as both an ingress and egress gateway for agent environments, routing the inbound traffic and restricting outbound network calls to verified domains and preventing untrusted autonomous code from reaching unauthorized endpoints. Getting started Envoy has evolved into an intelligent, extensible networking layer designed specifically for the unique demands of multi-agent architectures. To begin building with the agentic stack in Envoy: Explore the code: Review the Envoy proxy and Agent Router implementations on Github and examine the open-source sample configurations. Join the community: Participate in CNCF, Gateway API , and Kubernetes AI Gateway Working Group to collaborate on standardized inference APIs, MCP routing specifications, and token management conventions.

Envoy, an open-source edge and service proxy designed for cloud-native applications, has already transformed microservices and modern cloud networking, powering everything from Google Cloud’s Application Load Balancers to the Agent Substrate dataplane on Google Kubernetes Engine. Now, Envoy is uniquely positioned to become the open standard for AI traffic, MCP tooling, and agent-to-agent communication. Earlier this year, we presented the technical case for Envoy networking in the agentic AI era , examining how autonomous AI agents fundamentally challenge traditional Layer 7 networking assumptions.

title: Scaling massive AI/ML workloads with IPv6 on Google Kubernetes Engine clusters
raw_text:
TL;DR: Single-stack IPv6 on GKE runs both nodes and pods without having to use private IPv4 addresses. Available in preview for Cloud TPU v6e and CPU node pools, including Axion, it works with DNS64/NAT64 to reach IPv4 endpoints. Long before they run out of compute or power, AI applications hit another wall: running out of IP addresses. A single AI deployment often requires a vast address space to support everything from thousands of accelerator nodes, scaling inference replicas, bursting Ray workers and pipelines, pod sidecars, and services like vector databases. Running a dual stack — IPv6 behind a private IPv4 space — can help, but only to a point, because the private IPv4 space has often already been exhausted across existing networks. To help, today, we're announcing single-stack IPv6 on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), allowing you to run both nodes and pods on IPv6, without private IPv4 addresses. Single-stack IPv6 is available in preview for Cloud TPU v6e and CPU node pools, including Axion, and works with DNS64/NAT64 to reach IPv4 endpoints. Nodes and pods run IPv6-only across Cloud TPU v6e and CPU-based node pools, with no private IPv4. Workloads reach Google Cloud APIs over native IPv6 and IPv4-only endpoints through DNS64/NAT64. What single-stack IPv6 delivers The availability of single-stack IPv6 in GKE is a game-changer for large AI deployments. Consider the following features and benefits that it brings to the table: 1. No private IPv4 required for nodes or pods Nodes and pods use IPv6 exclusively. Without the RFC 1918 footprint that governs private IPv4 address spaces, clusters avoid conflicts with on-premises networks, peered VPCs, or adjacent clusters. 2. IPv4 interoperability with DNS64/NAT64 You enable DNS64 on the VPC, and NAT64 on a regional Cloud NAT gateway, allowing pods to transparently reach IPv4-only endpoints, registries, and dataset hubs — refer to the documentation to learn how to configure DNS64 and set up Cloud NAT . 3. Massive address space per node Each node receives a /112 pod range (65,536 addresses), so IP address capacity no longer limits how high your clusters, nodes, or pods can scale. Standard GKE maximum-pods-per-node limits still apply. 4. Broad accelerator and compute support We designed single-stack IPv6 in GKE with the goal of supporting a range of accelerators and general compute families. At preview, it supports Cloud TPU v6e (Trillium), plus E2, N1, N2, N2D, N4, C3, C3D, C4, C4D, C4A, and Z3 machine families, with support for additional accelerators and machine families coming soon. 5. Direct workload observability Every pod has a unique IPv6 address without having to run NAT inside the cluster, simplifying telemetry, network policies, and debugging. Performance and scale Single-stack IPv6 removes private IPv4 address limits without additional data plane overhead. In our internal testing, we saw the following performance characteristics: Pod lifecycle: Burst pod scheduling and CNI sandbox setup performed at parity with IPv4. Networking : Inter-node TCP/UDP latency and multi-stream pod-to-pod throughput matched IPv4. Services and DNS : eBPF service load balancing and NodeLocalDNS showed no measurable overhead compared to standard IPv4. Start building today Single-stack IPv6 is available now in preview on GKE version 1.37.1-gke.3020000 To create your first IPv6-only cluster, run the following commands, replacing REGION and CLUSTER_NAME: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# 1. Create a VPC with internal (ULA) IPv6 enabled
gcloud compute networks create gke-ipv6-net \
 --subnet-mode=custom \
 --enable-ula-internal-ipv6

# 2. Enable DNS64 for the VPC
gcloud dns policies create gke-ipv6-dns64 \
 --networks=gke-ipv6-net \
 --enable-dns64-all-queries

# 3. Enable NAT64 in your region
gcloud compute routers create gke-ipv6-router \
 --network=gke-ipv6-net --region=REGION
gcloud compute routers nats create gke-ipv6-nat64 \
 --router=gke-ipv6-router --region=REGION \
 --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips \
 --nat64-all-v6-subnet-ip-ranges

# 4. Create the cluster
gcloud beta container clusters create CLUSTER_NAME \
 --cluster-version=1.37.1-gke.3020000 \
 --location=REGION \
 --enable-dataplane-v2 \
 --cluster-dns=clouddns \
 --stack-type=ipv6 \
 --network=gke-ipv6-net \
 --create-subnetwork name=my-subnet \
 --ipv6-access-type=internal'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f467894ac90>)])]> To learn more, see the documentation .

Available in preview for Cloud TPU v6e and CPU node pools, including Axion, it works with DNS64/NAT64 to reach IPv4 endpoints. title: Testing changes, fast: Introducing agentic assessments in Database Center
raw_text: Applying recommendations to a production database can feel risky if you can’t easily quantify the performance benefit or justify the additional cost. While Database Center flags fleet-level health issues and provides proactive recommendations, database administrators still face the challenge of testing recommended changes without disrupting live applications or spending hours manually configuring staging replicas. To help solve this problem, we’re excited to announce the preview of assessments in Database Center for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL . Assessments is an agentic workflow that lets you run automated, isolated synthetic benchmarks on cloned instances, helping you verify potential performance gains before touching your production environment. Moving from recommendations to production changes Managing production databases means balancing system stability, performance, and infrastructure spend. When Database Center alerts you to a potential bottleneck and recommends a change, you need to evaluate the change before you can implement it. That workflow can be complex: Setting up dedicated staging environments to mirror production settings Running benchmark workloads to simulate real-world traffic Measuring latency, throughput, and resource saturation before and after applying changes Calculating whether performance gains justify potential cost adjustments Because this manual benchmarking process takes a lot of time and engineering effort, it’s easy to put off making critical updates, leaving databases under-provisioned or inefficient. How assessments automates the validation workflow Assessments simplify performance validation by automating the entire testing cycle in an isolated environment. When you click "Assess impact" on a supported recommendation in Database Center, the assessments workflow handles each step of the benchmarking process: Plan creation: Assessments builds a customized test plan for running a synthetic benchmark tailored to your instance. You can refine parameters such as client connections, transaction counts, query mode, or benchmark duration using plain-language prompts to match your target workload requirements (for example, "Change the benchmark duration to 60 seconds" ). Safe isolation: The agentic workflow clones your primary instance so that benchmarks run without consuming production resources or affecting live traffic. Baseline measurement: The workflow automatically runs synthetic workloads against the cloned instance to establish performance metrics from before the change. Applying changes: The workflow modifies the cloned environment according to the selected recommendation. Comparative reporting: Finally, it reruns the benchmark workload and generates an evaluation report comparing pre- and post-change metrics, including transaction throughput, average latency, CPU utilization, and memory usage — and automatically deletes the temporary clone once the assessment completes. Initial supported recommendations During the preview, you can run automated assessments for three types of Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL updates: Machine upgrade: Measure how increased vCPU and memory allocations impact query throughput and reduce compute contention under load. Edition upgrade: Compare performance metrics between Cloud SQL Enterprise and Enterprise Plus editions to verify throughput gains and reduced latency. Enable data cache: Evaluate how enabling data cache on Enterprise Plus instances affects read latency and offloads I/O bottlenecks for data-intensive workloads. Get started Assessments in Database Center are available in preview. You can start validating performance changes in your Cloud SQL for Postgres environment today directly in the Google Cloud console: Review the release notes for the latest updates on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Read the assessments overview to explore architecture details and supported database versions. Follow the step-by-step guide to create an assessment for your instances in Database Center.

title: How to Build Durable Agentic Systems with Google Antigravity: From Instructions to Loops
raw_text:
I watched the discussion on agentic loops grow louder over the past few months. But for me, the reality is simpler: prompt engineering has shifted from individual tasks to systems design, and the harness around the model (not the model itself) is now my primary constraint in software engineering. In this article, I'll show you how to build and verify those harnesses so you can move from single-turn instructions to durable agentic loops in Google Antigravity . Not all tasks are equal You can categorize the work that we give to our agents into five distinct tiers, scaling from a quick question up through Agile tasks, stories, and epics to a continuous system: A simple question : This does not require an agent; an assistant can answer it. A task / idea: This is one where a single prompt can zero-shot it. Use Google AI Studio to quickly transform ideas to functional prototypes. An app / larger feature / story: The kind of work that required weekly planning and splitting into subtasks before AI. Use loops for execution and full-featured agents, like Google Antigravity. This tier is also where your steering moves upstream: You lock in the spec, the plan, and the executable tests before any loop runs. A project / epic: A few features that make a cohesive story when connected. Loops here might help with planning too. This is also where one needs to go beyond simple turn-based prompting. A system : An overview of all of the projects and tasks. This is where you write AGENTS.md project instructions, create skills , set up sidecars , wire up verification gates, and configure an instrument cluster to keep themselves on top of everything. Loops at this level make the biggest difference and come with similarly higher risks. Figure 1: Five tiers of engineering work, from single prompts to verified agentic loops. Why the loop? The baseline of software development is shifting. This shift represents a basic law of human nature: we seek the highest leverage possible, moving from manual labor to delegation, and finally to orchestration. Because attention is the new bottleneck, anything that lets the work continue with less interruption could make a move in the right direction. By early 2026, empirical research of open-source projects estimated that coding agent adoption had reached between 22% and 29% of more than 128,000 active repositories on GitHub. Those who become proficient in agentic workflows now operate with a level of leverage that elevates their entire team's productivity. However, it also increases the cognitive load on everyone who is taking responsibility at the systemic level. To understand this shift, let's trace the technical lineage of loops and set some high level expectations. Academic foundations The academic seed was Yao et al.'s ReAct paper in October 2022, which interleaved reasoning traces with tool calls. ReAct beat reinforcement learning baselines by 34% on ALFWorld and 10% on WebShop by reasoning before acting, mirroring human nature: we perform better when verbalizing plans. Then came AutoGPT in early 2023, raising millions in venture funding. While early iterations of ReAct frequently spun in infinite loops, it proved developers wanted hands-off automation, highlighting the need for structural guardrails. Stateless experimentation In mid-2025, developers ran stateless bash loops that piped prompts into command-line agents and reset context files on every tick. Resetting context prevents cognitive bloat and acknowledges that human memory limits also apply to models. Stateless bash loops worked only because the durable state lived outside the model: in Git history, in progress files, and in the test suite. It successfully built self-hosting compilers over months of automated runs. By spring 2026, major tool environments absorbed this pattern, shipping native commands like /goal to let agents run unattended loops. The mathematics of autonomy Consider a theoretical example: If you put your agent in a flat sequential chain to complete multiple tasks in a row, the agent's success rate degrades exponentially. When each of its individual steps operates as an independent probability event, a sequence of N steps has a cumulative success rate of p N . For instance, if you run a task requiring 20 consecutive file modifications with a model that has p = 0.95 accuracy, then you face a success rate of only 36% . Without your structural interventions, they will fail almost certainly. Is 0.95 a real number? Treat it as an illustrative per-step reliability, not as a benchmark result. Even a frontier model reaches reliable multi-step outcomes only when it runs inside a verified harness. If your own per-step reliability sits closer to 75%, then the raw chain is already under 6% by step 10. The verification around the model sets the ceiling, which is why the loop matters. This is why you need evaluation loops. A verification gate should not force your agent to retry indefinitely (which causes infinite spinning runaways). Instead, it should pinpoint where the error occurred and allow the model exactly one targeted retry to fix it. If your agent has a 95% base accuracy, and your evaluation loop has a 95% chance of spotting and fixing the error on that single retry, the effective step success probability rises to 0.95 + (0.05 x 0.95) = 99.75% . That arithmetic assumes the check is independent of the worker, so the gate has to be an outside check. Compilers, test suites, and linters give you that for free, and behavioral evaluations let you assert on discrete tool calls and intermediate actions in seconds instead of waiting on a full end-to-end benchmark. For semantic judgments that a deterministic test cannot make, I pair models from different families so the reviewer does not share the worker's blind spot. Even if fixing fails, just spotting the error with a 95% accuracy, lets you jump in and manually realign the system while keeping the same 99.75% subagent accuracy and only paying the cost of human-in-the-loop intervention. The table below shows the probability of completion across different chain lengths, comparing raw models to this single-retry course-correction topology: Chain Length 95% Accuracy 95% x 95% Loop 3 Steps 86% 99% 5 Steps 77% 99% 10 Steps 60% 98% 15 Steps 46% 96% 20 Steps 36% 95% 30 Steps 21% 93% 50 Steps 8% 88% What about context bloat? If each step in a chain adds approximately 1% of context in tokens, you end up with a chain that is not much longer than 50 steps before we require compression. A 95% base accuracy that can be evaluated (and course corrected with 95% accuracy for each dimension that we care about) should keep you at good success rates for such individual running agents. If you establish a scalable way to divide and conquer problems, you can apply similar principles to drive your subagents. As we can see, at 20 steps, a 95% accuracy paired with a single-retry corrective loop yields a 95% end-to-end success rate (assuming the correction itself stays under our 20 steps soft limit) while keeping context size reasonable. Note that there is no explicit requirement for the correction to be AI or human driven, but rather it needs to produce accurate and verifiable results. This is where you divide problems into tasks that require a small number of steps each. If a problem is more complex, it remains approachable, but it must be divided into smaller subproblems, and so on. For our example, this means allocating up to 20 steps for each level agent, task, and trajectory and another 20 steps for the next level supervisory agent to consolidate contributions. To prevent drift, establish separate evaluations at all subagent and supervisory levels with a final acceptance criteria. Lastly, you must evaluate these metrics at least once for each level to verify that they measure the right target before running automation at a higher level. These are general estimations, but help you quickly decide whether you should split a problem, repeat a step, or commit results and move on. In practice, your numbers will look different, but the scaling laws will be similar. How to build a durable system What started as a source of friction has now become one of my primary driving curiosities: how do we build automation when we still have a lot to learn about the craft itself? I have a few ideas. To build a loop that does not run off a cliff, you must establish core guardrails that will keep accuracy high and will allow us to debug and intervene whenever necessary. Specifically, these are the pillars I identified: Durable state : Git-backed checkpoints ensure that your agent can resume work after a crash. Verification gates : Automated test suites and compilers deterministically check that the changes are correct. Write the acceptance criteria and the tests upstream, before implementation starts, and make one rule explicit in your project instructions: an agent cannot pass a gate by deleting or weakening a test. When done properly, gates can have >95% accuracy. However, you should be on the lookout for edge cases you might have forgotten about. Especially if verification, evaluation, or manual validation success rates diverge for any of your features. Evals : Anything that cannot be deterministically verified but is important should have an evaluation or benchmark which you can later inspect for accuracy. Try to write them in a way that will keep answers to a simple yes or no and accuracy high, ideally over 95%. If you're getting results that point to confusion or unexpected failures, you probably need to split the criteria into simpler ones. Halt conditions : Turn limits (as we saw above, 20 seems to be the sweet spot) and token or dollar cost ceilings stop runs before API budgets get out of control. Standardized skills and instructions : Reusable utilities, documented in the SKILL.md format, preferably bundled with code and source of truth references. Pair them with an AGENTS.md that holds the project invariants every run load. Skills stay on disk until their description matches the task, so they do not eat into the 20-step context window. These pillars don't name a model version, but rather a model family. Individual model leads last only weeks. The asset that survives each release is the harness and its processes: the AGENTS.md instructions every run loads, the SKILL.md modules loaded only when relevant, the isolated Cloud Run sandbox where the loop runs around the clock, the deterministic checks, and the cross-model review. When a run fails or you have to intervene, patch your harness along with the code: a new test, a line in AGENTS.md , a note in the skill. The next run inherits the lesson even though its context starts from zero. Platform built-in systems Platforms like Google Antigravity have codified these patterns ( /grill-me and /goal ) into built-in primitives, shifting the work from custom scripts to platform capabilities for most straightforward use cases. The same harness files travel with the repository whether you run Google Antigravity 2.0, the agy CLI, or Antigravity inside VS Code, JetBrains, or Cursor. I would encourage you to give these a try. Do remember, however, to keep an eye on trajectory lengths and look for model confusion. I myself frequently rely on the /goal primitives in Google Antigravity 2.0 when coordinating multi-turn tasks that require extensive validation and measurements before completion. To anchor this execution, use the /grill-me command for an interactive interview to lock in design constraints, invariants, and the tests that decide success before running /goal loops. Constructing the metrics for this technical article and then editing it is just one example of how I use these execution loops. By pairing /goal with /grill-me , you can establish an effective pair-programming dynamic: alignment on intent, followed by autonomy in execution. Custom DIY loops To understand the evolution of loops, compare two distinct architectures for DIY agentic loops: Stateless five-liner Geoffrey Huntley's "Ralph" loop is a prime example of stateless architecture. Here's the simplest working version of an Antigravity CLI loop: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'limit=20
for ((i=1; i<=limit; i++)); do
 agy -p "$(cat prompt.md)" --sandbox || break
 ./commit-and-test && break
done'), ('language', 'lang-py'), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f46789ce1d0>)])]> While simple, the stateless loop is fragile for multi-file coordination because resetting context discards thinking logs. A good agent skill could fix much of this limitation by instructing the model to output relevant progress reports in wiki-like markdown files and track changes by looking at git logs. Still, this complexity has led to developer challenges in larger multi-agent environments, for which custom loops seem to hold the promise. So what if you want to go to the deep end? If you want to write a custom loop from scratch, here is a practical Python implementation using the Google Antigravity SDK . Specifically, this loop does the following actions: Initializes a supervisor session. Executes a task. Verifies the output with the real test suite. Feeds the actual failure output back for exactly one targeted retry. Enforces strict call and token budgets. Not every task inside it is equal, so neither is the model. The supervisor and the implementer run on Gemini 4 Carbon because orchestration, architecture, and the complex fixes need frontier reasoning, codebase search goes to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and verification goes to a deterministic script that costs no tokens at all. The Guide to AI Tokenomics covers the budgeting side of this split. Far from being a production-ready solution, this is an experimental starting point that you can adapt to suit your individual needs: Figure 2: Budgeted supervisory verification loop in the Google Antigravity SDK. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'import asyncio
import subprocess

from google.antigravity import Agent, LocalAgentConfig, types
from google.antigravity.hooks import policy

def verify_output(workspace_path: str) -> tuple[bool, str]:
 """Verification gate: run the test suite and keep the real failure output."""
 result = subprocess.run(
 ["go", "test", "./..."], cwd=workspace_path, capture_output=True, text=True
 )
 output = (result.stdout + "\n" + result.stderr).strip()
 return result.returncode == 0, output

# 1. Define subagents with scoped tools and a model that fits each job
researcher = types.SubagentConfig(
 name="researcher",
 description="Searches the codebase and summarizes implementation paths.",
 system_instructions=(
 "You are a research subagent. Analyze the codebase, find implementation "
 "paths, and report back without modifying any files."
 ),
 model="gemini-4-hydrogen",
 capabilities=types.SubagentCapabilities(
 enabled_tools=[
 types.BuiltinTools.VIEW_FILE,
 types.BuiltinTools.SEARCH_DIR,
 types.BuiltinTools.FIND_FILE,
 ],
 ),
)

feature_implementer = types.SubagentConfig(
 name="feature_implementer",
 description="Implements a scoped code change and keeps the tests passing.",
 system_instructions=(
 "You are a feature implementation subagent. Follow AGENTS.md, write "
 "clean code, run the tests, and fix compiler errors. Never delete or "
 "weaken a test to make it pass."
 ),
 model="gemini-4-carbon",
 capabilities=types.SubagentCapabilities(
 enabled_tools=[
 types.BuiltinTools.VIEW_FILE,
 types.BuiltinTools.EDIT_FILE,
 types.BuiltinTools.CREATE_FILE,
 types.BuiltinTools.RUN_COMMAND,
 ],
 ),
)

# 2. Expose both subagents to the supervisor, with a 20-call and token budget
supervisor_config = LocalAgentConfig(
 model="gemini-4-carbon",
 workspaces=["./workspace"],
 subagents=[researcher, feature_implementer],
 policies=[policy.allow_all()],
 budget_config=types.BudgetConfig(
 max_model_calls=20,
 max_total_tokens=200_000,
 ),
 system_instructions=(
 "You are a supervisor agent. Delegate codebase exploration to "
 "@researcher and code changes to @feature_implementer. Summarize each "
 "completed step before moving on."
 ),
)

async def run_agentic_loop(prompt: str, max_retries: int = 1) -> bool:
 """Supervisory loop. We only instantiate and run the supervisor explicitly."""
 async with Agent(supervisor_config) as supervisor:
 for attempt in range(1, max_retries + 2):
 print(f"[Supervisor Loop] Attempt {attempt}/{max_retries + 1}...")

 # Send prompt to the supervisor; it spawns subagents autonomously as needed
 response = await supervisor.chat(prompt)
 await response.text() # Drain the stream before reading the stop reason

 # Halt condition: the SDK stops the turn when a budget is exceeded
 if response.stop_reason in (
 types.StopReason.MAX_MODEL_CALLS_EXCEEDED,
 types.StopReason.MAX_TOTAL_TOKENS_EXCEEDED,
 ):
 print(f"Loop halted: budget exceeded ({response.stop_reason}).")
 return False

 usage = supervisor.conversation.total_usage
 print(f"Tokens used so far: {usage.total_token_count or 0:,} / 200,000")

 # Verification gate: deterministic, and independent of the worker
 success, error_msg = verify_output("./workspace")
 if success:
 print("Goal completed: verification gate passed.")
 return True

 # Exactly one targeted retry, with the real failure output
 prompt = (
 "The previous attempt failed verification with the following output:\n"
 f"{error_msg}\n"
 "Delegate a targeted fix to @feature_implementer and run the tests again."
 )

 print("Verification still failing after the retry. Handing over to a human.")
 return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
 asyncio.run(run_agentic_loop("Refactor types.go to use explicit interfaces."))'), ('language', 'lang-py'), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f46793def50>)])]> The preceding implementation defines the following budgets: max_model_calls=20 , a soft limit, counted across the supervisor's whole session max_total_tokens=200_000 as the cost ceiling The SDK stops the turn and reports a stop_reason when either one trips. max_retries=1 limits each section: the first attempt plus one fix. If the verification still fails after that, the loop returns False and a human takes the seat instead of the model spinning until the budget runs out. If you prefer not to build and host your own custom SDK loops from scratch, use Antigravity Agent , an autonomous, asynchronous coding agent. Antigravity Agent operates in a secure, isolated Google Cloud sandbox. This way you can create similar agentic loops by using managed agents to orchestrate execution plans under Google managed infrastructure. Alternatively, you can run the preceding loop inside a long-lived Cloud Run sandbox so that the loop keeps working after you close your laptop. No one size fits all You must establish a clear boundary for each of your validation systems that lets you stay in control. No matter how perfect your loop, if you , as the responsible human, cannot sign off on your agent's output, there is minimal value in any of the artifacts it is producing. The good news is that building a quality evaluation scorecard or a loop algorithm uses a similar process to producing any other type of software artifact. So, much of the execution will be automated. Finally, to make a sound judgment, you should observe each loop from the inside. As you see things working out, with this acquired confidence you step one level up. This is the only way to learn where the agent struggles and how to improve the process itself.

title: Simplifying multicloud networking to Azure with partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect
raw_text: As AI changes how businesses build and run applications, more enterprises are spreading their models, data and applications across multiple clouds. To make that work, they need fast, private connections between those environments. Historically, connecting multiple clouds has meant ordering physical connections from each provider, setting up networking on both sides, and coordinating across multiple teams. That process could take weeks or even months. We wanted to make that much simpler. Today, we're extending partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect to Microsoft Azure, now available in preview. The service is jointly supported by Google Cloud and Microsoft, and gives you a private, high-bandwidth connection between your Google Cloud and Azure environments that’s set up programmatically in minutes, with no physical infrastructure to manage. "Google Cloud partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect simplifies multi-cloud networking with a direct cloud-native approach. By removing traditional infrastructure complexity, it provides a reliable, scalable foundation for connecting workloads across different cloud environments." - Ralf Huebenthal, Global Head of IT & Digital Platforms, Nestlé “Walmart runs a seamless platform across multiple cloud providers to accelerate innovations. We partner with Google Cloud to leverage their global network for hybrid and multicloud networking. With Cross-Cloud Interconnect, we were able to simplify connectivity between cloud providers, shorten time to production, and reduce overall costs.” - Gerald Bothello, Group Director of Software Engineering, Walmart Partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect benefits On-demand connectivity in minutes, not weeks. Set up your connection from the Google Cloud console or API, pick the bandwidth you need, and both clouds handle the rest — no hardware to order, no manual network configuration, and no back and forth between providers. Built-in reliability. Your connection runs across physically separate locations for redundancy. Google Cloud and Azure jointly monitor the connection and handle maintenance and recovery for you. Private and secure. Your traffic stays off the public internet, and is automatically encrypted between the Google Cloud and Azure edge routers, with no customer configuration required. Predictable pricing. You pay a fixed price for the connection's bandwidth, so your Google Cloud costs are easy to plan and manage. "Customers are building applications, data platforms and AI across more than one cloud, and they want the network between those clouds to just work. Azure Multicloud Interconnect with Google Cloud gives customers a private, managed path between Azure and Google Cloud, and we're excited to work with Google Cloud to bring it to customers in public preview." - Sudha Mahajan, Partner, Product Management, Azure Networking, Microsoft Our Cross-Cloud Interconnect ecosystem continues to expand: Partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect for Microsoft Azure is available in preview today in us-east4 (N. Virginia), us-west2 (Los Angeles), and europe-west3 (Frankfurt), alongside the generally available AWS and OCI offerings. We'll add more regions as the Azure offering moves to general availability. Partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect for last mile with Lumen is available in preview, for customers connecting their private clouds, on-premises sites, and neocloud environments to Google Cloud. Partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect is built on an open specification for network interoperability. Google Cloud collaborated with AWS and published it last year, and any provider can adopt it. To learn more, visit the partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect documentation , read Microsoft's announcement , or contact your Google Cloud account team.

title: Google Cloud is a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Application Development Platforms
raw_text: For the third time in a row, Google Cloud is recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Application Development Platforms , positioned highest overall on the Ability to Execute axis. 1 These days, it’s very clear to us that organizations are looking for AI to handle actual day-to-day work, stay strictly within compliance guardrails, and deliver measurable ROI. In the last year, nearly 500 Google Cloud customers each processed more than one trillion tokens . And a lot of that volume came from heavily regulated sectors like global banking, healthcare, and telecommunications. Our customers choose Gemini because it delivers an open enterprise platform built for this level of production scale, by: Unifying the agent experience across everyday workflows Providing unrestricted model choice without vendor lock-in Practicing cost discipline before bills spiral, not after Governing agents through a single, centralized control plane 1. Gemini delivers one universal agent across the enterprise In October, we announced a unified Gemini experience. The same Gemini you collaborate with every day is now your enterprise agent to get real work done. Instead of navigating disconnected developer consoles, consumer tools, and workplace add-ons, Gemini meets work wherever it already happens – collaborating natively inside surfaces like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, internal chats, web, and mobile. You give Gemini high-level business objectives rather than step-by-step instructions, and it orchestrates the necessary tools, context, and coworker agents to deliver a finished result. As employees engage it, the agent retains persistent memory, understands your specific business language, and respects enterprise permissions across every device. When a team automates a complex procedure, they can package it into a shared skill, turning one group’s procedural knowledge into a capability anyone across the organization can use. That shared foundation is what transforms agent building from an isolated engineering backlog into an organization-wide capability. At Dojo , one of UK’s leading payment providers, non-technical teams used this exact environment to stand up over 600 custom agents in just two months: “When you can use natural language, anyone from HR to sales can turn their unique business experience into a custom AI agent in minutes. In two months, we created over 600 agents. The majority were built by our frontline business teams right inside Gemini, leaving our developers to focus on more complex challenges.” – Robert Howes, Chief Technology Officer, Dojo. Dojo fuels an AI-native future, delivers 680+ agents in two months with Gemini Dojo fuels an AI-native future, delivers 680+ agents in two months with Gemini 2. We bring the leading frontier models under one roof Google Cloud is now the only hyperscale cloud provider offering access to all three leading frontier model families, from Google, Anthropic and OpenAI, on a unified enterprise platform – and across every surface, from developer tooling in Antigravity to everyday productivity in Gemini for web, mobile, and desktop. Through the model garden, organizations can access over 200 models, drawing down existing cloud commitments on a single invoice without having to negotiate separate contracts. At the same time, we are deeply proud of the pace of innovation coming out of Google DeepMind. Over the past month alone, we’ve rolled out a full generation of specialized models: Gemini 4 Argon for strong performance across complex software engineering, law, finance, and cyber defense; Gemini 4 Carbon for frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows; and now Gemini 4 Hydrogen , bringing cutting-edge intelligence with speed and efficiency to everyday coding and agentic execution. By treating models as a diversified portfolio, we give our customers the freedom to optimize for speed, precision, and cost across every task. For PayPal , this flexibility is central to their strategy: “We built a unified LLM stack. That meant we ran our open source models on top of our inferencing stack on GKE, and we ran our close-sourced models on top of the Gemini platform. Developers get choice – Claude, Gemini, Open Source – through one consistent governed access layer. That’s why we love the model garden.” — Srinivasan Manoharan, Director of AI/ML Platform, PayPal. PayPal paves the way for the future of agentic commerce with Google Cloud PayPal paves the way for the future of agentic commerce with Google Cloud 3. Optimizing spend at every layer of the stack A recurring concern we hear from enterprise leaders is the unpredictability of AI billing. When teams start scaling agents, pay-as-you-go pricing can feel like an open tab with no ceiling. That is why we optimize cost across every layer of the stack – co-designing custom TPU silicon, cluster networking, and foundation models as a single system to drive down baseline costs. At the execution level, we give finance and engineering teams the right levers to innovate without risking their margins. Gemini dynamically matches every task to the most cost-effective model, handling high-volume tasks with efficient models, only escalating to frontier reasoning models for complex problem-solving. Paired with native FinOps controls – including project-level monthly spend caps, anomaly detection, and Flexible Savings Plans – leaders get hard financial boundaries and clear visibility. For companies processing massive volumes of data, this approach makes all the difference. At Imgix , the engineering team prioritized this architectural discipline as they scaled visual processing: “If we're using the most expensive model every single time, that's going to be a big bill for our customers. That same control plane extends to how agents interact with corporate intelligence. Rather than requiring organizations to move, replicate, or duplicate sensitive records into yet another external repository, Gemini connects directly to live enterprise systems.
