title: How sovereign do we need to be? Data sovereignty as a spectrum
raw_text:
The US Cloud Act and FISA 702 give Washington the power to compel US companies to hand over data, wherever it sits. Meanwhile, Five Eyes intelligence sharing widens potential data snooping to US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand collaboration.

So, what sovereignty guarantees remain when such mechanisms potentially allow cloud data to be accessed by law or bilateral agreement, and when a US provider can be compelled to write or push a patch into systems anywhere in the world?

That’s the question Google executives were asked at its Sovereign AI Summit in Brussels this week, where the company argued sovereignty is a spectrum and that customers should choose their point on it.

Jai Haridas, vice-president of regulated and sovereign cloud at Google Cloud, did not dodge the legal point. “We are a US company, and we have to follow the US laws,” he said.

But he pointed to architectural responses made possible in Google white-labelling of its technology to national cloud offerings. There aren’t many deployments to point at, but one is PREMI3NS – a sovereign cloud offering built on Google Cloud Dedicated technology and operated by S3NS – which received SecNumCloud 3.2 qualification from France’s National Agency for the Security of Information Systems (ANSSI) in 2025.

Under SecNumCloud, for example, “all updates go into quarantine where they are tested by the operator Thales, and they can actually stop an update”, Haridas said.

If there’s a spectrum, such measures are near the strong end of it.

At the summit, Google announced functionality that aims to make such a spectrum realistic for customers. These included a preview of confidential external (ie, customer) key management and audit frameworks, which extend the three-tier sovereign portfolio – data boundary, dedicated cloud and distributed cloud – it launched last year.

Meanwhile, analysts at Omdia are working on a five-level maturity model to help organisations work out where they sit:

  1. At level one, sovereignty is not a focus. We find reliance on third-party infrastructure, in unregulated firms with speed and cost unrestricted by sovereignty concerns.
  2. Level two offers improved visibility, but still no control, through public cloud offers that add privacy and guaranteed local residency features.
  3. Level three describes regulated industries that are still mostly reliant on cloud provider infrastructure but may need direct control over critical data and software via sovereign cloud solutions where law and regulation compel them.
  4. Level four gives public bodies with high geopolitical sensitivity – such as in the public sector – direct control over the full stack through a local partner that operates the same code base as the cloud provider, with extra-territorial access still in place.
  5. Level five is “very strong” with full control of data, software and infrastructure via national cloud providers or air-gapped solutions, and is reserved for organisations where the fundamentals of their activity would be at stake, such as defence organisations or Swiss banks.

Panel contributors at the event (pictured above) showed how such a spectrum accords with real-world practice.

Gertjan Dewaele, vice-president of product and technology at payment product company Worldline, described its dual setup – global payment workloads on public cloud, and a sovereign European stack for clients and projects such as the digital euro.

“Sovereignty for payments is not new,” he said. Regulation already pushes in this direction, such as under Dora, the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act, where financial firms must show exit plans and fully redundant systems.

Roman Kislyi from Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation described the far end of the spectrum. His ministry runs Gemini but strips out identifying data before it leaves the country, while keeping critical systems in distributed datacentres and a data embassy located abroad.

“Will your solution save the data of your citizens? Will your solution work if your datacentres are hit by a missile? Will your solution work if there is a blackout? Those are the questions we ask ourselves every day,” Kislyi said.

For manufacturers, the trade-off is different. Hamza Charrouf, chief customer officer at Pelico, said industrial customers want to keep operational knowledge out of models they do not control, and increasingly want innovation and sovereignty together rather than have to make a choice between them.

Panel members converged on a single point – the right level of control depends on what the data is for. “Take the emotion out of the domain, understand what you need, and then develop that,” said Robert Kernahan, vice-president and head of sovereign cloud for northern and central Europe at Capgemini.

“And when you break away from this one-size-fits-all idea, you go to optionality of choice, and you build that in,” he said.

Marcus Mühling, chief executive of Secure Cloud Germany, put the same point more bluntly. “If your clients have to make extreme choices – either sovereignty or innovation – that’s broken,” he said.

But cost is a key constraint. A partner-operated dedicated cloud carries a premium of 15% to 20% above standard public cloud rates, Google’s Haridas said. He described it as “a luxury product if you don’t need it”, but not if regulation requires it.

Sovereignty is clearly moving up the stack towards artificial intelligence, although that wasn’t a major topic of many conversations at the event.

But, said Mauro Capo, digital sovereignty lead EMEA at Accenture, clients now often ask who controls the models, the enterprise knowledge they draw on, and “the decisions and the actions that those models will increasingly influence”. Sovereignty, he argued, is shifting from infrastructure to data and knowledge.

For UK IT leaders, the debate may have taken place on the continent, but the spectrum of responses exists here too. The UK Ministry of Defence runs Google’s air-gapped distributed cloud variant, for example, and UK organisations that use US hyperscalers face the same Cloud Act question but without any EU-type security certification as a response.

The practical lesson is the one the panel kept returning to: Classify the data, decide the level of control each class needs, and build exit routes in from the start.

Read more about data sovereignty

  • Data dive: Kill switch and catch-up – can Europe close the sovereignty gap? We examine whether European providers can match hyperscalers on continuity and control.

title: Unlawfully held images still used for police facial recognition
raw_text:
UK police are continuing to conduct tens of thousands of retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches on potentially millions of unlawfully retained custody images, the police watchdog has found.

In November 2026, the HM Chief Inspector of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS) published a 58-page report examining how police forces and the National Crime Agency (NCA) are using RFR, after being commissioned by UK home secretary Shabana Mahmood to investigate the matter a year earlier.

Unlike live facial recognition (LFR), which captures and compares people’s faces to a pre-determined watchlist in real time, RFR is applied to already-captured images retroactively, enabling police to compare “probe” images against existing custody images taken when suspects are arrested.

The Home Office originally added an a RFR function to the Police National Database (PND) in 2013, allowing trained and licensed police users to search custody images to identify unknown persons of interest.

As it stands, the PND – which collates data from all 43 police forces in England and Wales, as well as Police Scotland, the Police Service of Northern Ireland, the National Crime Agency and other law enforcement bodies – contains billions of records drawn from several hundred databases, including more than 20 million facial images.

According to the watchdog, its inspection revealed that custody images are still being retained in breach of police information management rules, which set out how forces should review, retain and dispose of custody images.

It noted that while custody image deletion was largely outside the scope of its inspection – which instead focused more on governance arrangements and operational practices – it nonetheless found that “some of the images used in RFR searches should have been deleted and yet were still available for RFR searches”.

It added that this creates a situation that “risks undermining public confidence” in how police are using the technology.

As it stands, UK law enforcement bodies are making more than 300,000 RFR search requests per year.

On top of issues around unlawful custody image retention, the watchdog also found that police use of RFR technology lacked consistent oversight and safeguards, describing a legal and regulatory landscape that is fragmented and underdeveloped.

The “limited oversight”, it added, is compounded by inconsistent approaches to public consultation, transparency and record-keeping across forces, as well as “considerable variation” in how individual forces are using the tech itself.

It also found that police forces often did not have enough management information to understand how effectively they used RFR, or to evaluate the technology’s contribution to crime investigations. This means forces generally “couldn’t clearly show performance improvements from using RFR”.

A long-standing issue

Although it is not mentioned in the report, a High Court ruling in 2012 found the retention of custody images in the PND to be unlawful, on the basis that information about unconvicted people was being treated in the same way as information about people who were ultimately convicted. It also ruled that the six-year retention period was disproportionate.

Despite the 2012 ruling, successive biometric commissioners have warned that millions of custody images are still being unlawfully retained.

Writing to other chief constables to outline some of the issues around custody image retention in February 2022, the National Police Chiefs Council (NPCC) lead for records management, Lee Freeman, said the potentially unlawful retention of millions of custody images “poses a significant risk in terms of potential litigation, police legitimacy and wider support and challenge in our use of these images for technologies such as facial recognition”.

However, HMICFRS said in its report that it was “reassured” by a project launched in October 2023 by the Home Office and NPCC – known as Programme Tabula – to manage the custody image retention issue.

Responding to Computer Weekly’s questions about the custody image issue in November 2023, the NPCC said at the time that “policing needs to ensure transparency and legitimacy in the way we control the use of this important biometric information.”

While a spokesperson confirmed that a national programme had been launched a month earlier “to ensure consistency and co-ordination across UK policing in how it retains, processes and then uses custody images, particularly in the use of facial recognition”, it did not disclose the name of the programme.

“Through the programme, we will agree and implement a robust management regime for custody images to ensure compliance to agreed policies and legislation,” it said. “It is vital to public confidence that this programme is adopted nationally to make sure we are holding data lawfully and ethically, both now and in the future.”

The spokesperson added that while the programme was yet to be publicised, it will seek to establish a management regime for custody images, alongside a review of all currently held data by police forces in the UK, which will be implemented over a two-year period.

“We welcome this work,” said HMICFRS. “It is important that the police service aligns its approach to retaining custody images with other biometric data so that it is consistent and lawful. We look forward to learning how Programme Tabula will support forces in managing custody images more consistently and improving their compliance with legal and data retention requirements.”

Limited oversight

In terms of the wider oversight issues, HMICFRS found that legislation has not kept up with the technology or its use, leading to governance gaps and inconsistent oversight practices.

“Some forces had clear guidance setting out how searches should be carried out, how results should be recorded and what corroborative enquiries were required,” it wrote. “Others lacked formal procedures, which increased the risk of inconsistent decision-making and misunderstanding of the technology’s limitations.

“We found that investigators and supervisors didn’t routinely document the consideration or use of RFR in investigation plans, enquiry logs or supervisory reviews. As a result, forces often lacked clear audit trails showing how RFR results informed decision-making and whether appropriate corroboration had taken place.

“This limits forces’ ability to assess their use of RFR, identify missed opportunities, and provide effective scrutiny and governance.”

On how this translates into practical use, HMICFRS said that police investigators did not always know that RFR results were intelligence rather than evidence, and therefore required further enquiries before officers took enforcement action.

“This creates a risk that people could be incorrectly identified or arrested, which could undermine public confidence in the technology,” it said.

“We found that some investigators didn’t always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches. In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.”

His Majesty’s Inspector of Constabulary Kathryn Stone said continued public support relied on showing the technology was being used properly.

“Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment,” she said. “A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence.”

Upcoming legislation

In December 2025, the Home Office launched a 10-week consultation on police use of biometrics, including LFR, allowing interested parties and members of the public to share their views on how the controversial technology should be regulated. This also covered other forms of biometric surveillance, including RFR.

This followed on from then-home secretary Yvette Cooper telling a Lords committee in July 2025 that the government intended to create “a proper, clear governance framework” to regulate the use of facial recognition technology by police.

When launching the consultation, the Home Office said that although a “patchwork” legal framework for police use of facial recognition technology exists – including for increasing use of retrospective and “operator-initiated” versions – it does not give police forces the confidence to “use it at significantly greater scale … nor does it consistently give the public the confidence that it will be used responsibly”.

While the government reiterated its intention to bring forward a new legislative framework for police use of biometrics in its formal consultation response, it has so far refrained from committing to specific safeguards, outside of establishing a new independent oversight body (which will consolidate and expand the functions of existing oversight roles) and committing to making public participation in oversight of a statutory requirement.

The government said the framework “will ensure policing can innovate in a repeatable and consistent manner, supporting adoption of emerging biometric and overt surveillance technologies that improve policing effectiveness and public protection, while maintaining appropriate safeguards and oversight”.

UK police are continuing to conduct tens of thousands of retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches on potentially millions of unlawfully retained custody images, the police watchdog has found.

In November 2026, the HM Chief Inspector of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS) published a 58-page report examining how police forces and the National Crime Agency (NCA) are using RFR, after being commissioned by UK home secretary Shabana Mahmood to investigate the matter a year earlier.

Unlike live facial recognition (LFR), which captures and compares people’s faces to a pre-determined watchlist in real time, RFR is applied to already-captured images retroactively, enabling police to compare “probe” images against existing custody images taken when suspects are arrested.

The Home Office originally added an a RFR function to the Police National Database (PND) in 2013, allowing trained and licensed police users to search custody images to identify unknown persons of interest.

As it stands, the PND – which collates data from all 43 police forces in England and Wales, as well as Police Scotland, the Police Service of Northern Ireland, the National Crime Agency and other law enforcement bodies – contains billions of records drawn from several hundred databases, including more than 20 million facial images.

According to the watchdog, its inspection revealed that custody images are still being retained in breach of police information management rules, which set out how forces should review, retain and dispose of custody images.

It noted that while custody image deletion was largely outside the scope of its inspection – which instead focused more on governance arrangements and operational practices – it nonetheless found that “some of the images used in RFR searches should have been deleted and yet were still available for RFR searches”.

It added that this creates a situation that “risks undermining public confidence” in how police are using the technology.

As it stands, UK law enforcement bodies are making more than 300,000 RFR search requests per year.

On top of issues around unlawful custody image retention, the watchdog also found that police use of RFR technology lacked consistent oversight and safeguards, describing a legal and regulatory landscape that is fragmented and underdeveloped.

The “limited oversight”, it added, is compounded by inconsistent approaches to public consultation, transparency and record-keeping across forces, as well as “considerable variation” in how individual forces are using the tech itself.

It also found that police forces often did not have enough management information to understand how effectively they used RFR, or to evaluate the technology’s contribution to crime investigations. This means forces generally “couldn’t clearly show performance improvements from using RFR”.

A long-standing issue

Although it is not mentioned in the report, a High Court ruling in 2012 found the retention of custody images in the PND to be unlawful, on the basis that information about unconvicted people was being treated in the same way as information about people who were ultimately convicted. It also ruled that the six-year retention period was disproportionate.

Despite the 2012 ruling, successive biometric commissioners have warned that millions of custody images are still being unlawfully retained.

Writing to other chief constables to outline some of the issues around custody image retention in February 2022, the National Police Chiefs Council (NPCC) lead for records management, Lee Freeman, said the potentially unlawful retention of millions of custody images “poses a significant risk in terms of potential litigation, police legitimacy and wider support and challenge in our use of these images for technologies such as facial recognition”.

However, HMICFRS said in its report that it was “reassured” by a project launched in October 2023 by the Home Office and NPCC – known as Programme Tabula – to manage the custody image retention issue.

Responding to Computer Weekly’s questions about the custody image issue in November 2023, the NPCC said at the time that “policing needs to ensure transparency and legitimacy in the way we control the use of this important biometric information.”

While a spokesperson confirmed that a national programme had been launched a month earlier “to ensure consistency and co-ordination across UK policing in how it retains, processes and then uses custody images, particularly in the use of facial recognition”, it did not disclose the name of the programme.

“Through the programme, we will agree and implement a robust management regime for custody images to ensure compliance to agreed policies and legislation,” it said. “It is vital to public confidence that this programme is adopted nationally to make sure we are holding data lawfully and ethically, both now and in the future.”

The spokesperson added that while the programme was yet to be publicised, it will seek to establish a management regime for custody images, alongside a review of all currently held data by police forces in the UK, which will be implemented over a two-year period.

“We welcome this work,” said HMICFRS.

title: Former Italian PM centre stage as Google champions EU sovereignty
raw_text:
Europe can no longer be “competitive, sovereign and small” at the same time, Enrico Letta told an audience in Brussels this week. The former Italian prime minister – and now dean of politics, economics, and global affairs at IE University in Madrid – was speaking at an event hosted by Google, rather than the European Parliament or a national capital.

“In the past, the discussion about sovereignty, dimension and competitiveness was a very simple discussion,” he said. “In the past, you were able to be competitive small, and sovereign at the same time. Today, you can’t be competitive, sovereign and small. You need to be integrated in something bigger, and this is what we need to do, to scale up.” 

Letta spoke at Google’s Sovereign AI Summit in Brussels this week, where the US hyperscaler argued that European strength and European sovereignty can advance together.

Marianne Janik, who leads Google Cloud’s operations across EMEA North, opened the event with a message that presaged Letta’s. “AI will shape the next decade of Europe’s public service, healthcare and finance, and has to happen under European control,” she said.

Janik said the same four questions surfaced “in conversation after conversation”. Namely: Who can access our data and can we prove to regulators that our controls work? How do we keep AI running reliably? Will choosing more control mean settling for less capable AI? And will the value created with AI stay in Europe?

Her answer was that Google can help organisations with all four of these. “Keep your options open at every layer,” she told delegates, describing a stack that customers can compose from European partners, open models and Google’s own infrastructure.

The company used the summit to put Gemini models into Google Cloud Dedicated, preview confidential external key management and add audit frameworks. These extend the three-tier sovereign portfolio – data boundary, dedicated cloud and distributed cloud – it launched last year. It also launched an accelerator for sovereign AI startups and said more than a dozen software suppliers, including European providers, had validated their products on its dedicated cloud.

Letta, author of the 2024 report Much more than a market, argued that Europe’s problem is fragmentation rather than a lack of ambition. He wants a “28th regime”, a European code of business law that lets firms scale across the bloc without 27 national rulebooks.

“I don’t want Europe being a protectionist fortress,” he said. “I would like to see Europe stronger, more integrated, able to recuperate 25 years of non-integration.”

He framed the debate around what he called the “cost of non-innovation”, borrowing from the 1988 Cecchini report on the cost of non-integration that underpinned the single market. The same method, he argued, should now apply to technology. Namely, every regulation that slows adoption carries a price that rarely appears on the ledger.

He was also clear that the answer is not to shut out US technology. “If you think that now we get total energy independence in one year, total financial independence in one year, total tech independence in one year, I think it’s totally unrealistic,” he said. Trust, he added, “is the most relevant value in our world”, and “mutual trust between Europe and the US is also politically fundamental”.

The politics turns on CADA, the Cloud and AI Development Act, which European institutions are still negotiating. Google’s stage guests warned that a restrictive reading would be expensive. Discussion cited an ECIPE paper that put the migration bill at €80bn across the next decade and warned of an eight-year delay to innovation.

The fault line is whether CADA should favour “made in Europe” providers or stay open to trusted non-European firms that operate through local partners. Google is lobbying hard for the latter, and its guests echoed the argument that exclusion would raise costs without improving security.

Giorgia Albetino, senior director and head of government affairs and public policy for Google Cloud EMEA, put it directly. “I don’t believe that only made-in-Europe will really serve the interests of Europeans,” she said.

The dependency argument ran through the event. Timo Kleiner, director of future networks at the European Commission, said “dependency is a problem” when a single provider fails. “Dependencies, when they are too significant, become risks,” he said, referring to the disruption caused by a global IT outage the previous week.

Marcus Mühling, chief executive of Secure Cloud Germany, put the customer view plainly: “If your clients have to make extreme choices – either sovereignty or innovation – that’s broken.”

The event was not a one-way conversation. Roy Illsley, an analyst at Omdia, read the display as a competitive move. “Google is trying to create a difference between its approach and their rivals,” he said. “They are playing the ‘open’ card, which has been under-used as a contingency or alternate supply.”

Oracle has Alloy, AWS has its European Sovereign Cloud, and Microsoft is “playing catch up”, Illsley argued. Google’s enthusiasm for European integration, on this reading, is a way to stand apart from the pack.

It might appear puzzling that a US hyperscaler would platform explicit European advocacy. But Google has a commercial interest in the outcome. A louder European voice on sovereignty helps shape CADA in a direction that keeps hyperscalers inside the tent, and it positions Google as the partner of choice for governments that want control without giving up frontier AI.

For UK IT leaders, the event matters less as a product launch than as a signal. UK CIOs should be watching how far CADA reaches, since many run workloads in EU regions and face the same questions about who can access data.

Google has brought an interesting pitch – a company subject to US law, arguing for European strategic autonomy. It has made the argument louder than its rivals and attached a product portfolio to it.

title: ANZ migrates 1.7 petabytes of data to Amazon Web Services
raw_text:
Australia and New Zealand Banking Group (ANZ) has created a foundation for its use of data, analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) after the successful migration of 1.7PB (petabytes) of data to Amazon Web Services (AWS).

The finance group finished the data migration in a third of the time expected through the use of AI-assisted engineering.

By moving to the AWS cloud platform, the bank aims to improve customer experiences and security.

The data migrated was part of ANZ’s on-premise Enterprise Big Data platform, which underpinned payments, business banking and customer remediation. The bank said the 1.7PB moved was equivalent to more than 340 million smartphone photos, comprising 300 million files, 142,000 tables, 4,500 automated data workflows and 4,000 views.

“The migration was completed in six months instead of an anticipated 18 months, using AI-assisted engineering to help analyse, convert, test and optimise workloads,” said ANZ. Engineers used a troubleshooting AI assistant powered by Amazon Bedrock to support their work. As a result, the bank said testing and validation reduced defects and rework by about 50%.

ANZ Group’s CIO, Donald Patra, said: “This transformation strengthens our technology foundations to make banking better and simpler for our customers. It also demonstrates how AI-assisted engineering can accelerate complex delivery while maintaining a disciplined focus on security, resilience and quality.”

In using the new platform, ANZ has reduced operating costs from more than A$10,000 per day to less than A$3,000 per month.

Data is the foundation of modern banking and increasingly the foundation of AI. As we explore new ways to use data and analytics to improve customer and employee experiences, having modern, scalable and secure infrastructure is critical,” said ANZ’s chief data and AI officer, Kai Yang.

“This transformation modernises one of ANZ’s most important data platforms and provides a stronger foundation for future innovation. It gives us greater flexibility to scale and simplify our technology environment and accelerate the development of new data and capabilities over time,” he added.

“Completing a programme of this scale in six months demonstrates what can be achieved when technology, people and AI-assisted engineering come together behind a shared goal,” said Yang.

The new platform will support ANZ’s 2030 Strategy, which aims to simplify the bank’s technology estate, modernise critical data infrastructure and establish the foundation to enable data and AI at scale.

Read more about AWS in finance: Billion-dollar AWS financial services investment builds on a decade of work

A decade ago, AWS found itself at the beginning of a revolution in the finance sector, with its on-demand cloud computing capacity piped into firms on a pay-as-you-consume basis. This set the foundations for the current AI-driven technology revolution.

But tech giants such as AWS now go beyond providing raw compute power and are providing hands-on experience and support to customers adopting the latest technologies, such as AI.

Chris Casey, AWS’s managing director for Australia and New Zealand, said: “Migrating a major banking data platform while it continues to serve customers in real time is one of the most complex undertakings in financial services. Completing a migration of this scale in six months reflects the trust and world-class delivery capability of AWS Professional Services, AWS Partners and the team at ANZ.”

title: Fujitsu’s UK government business exceeds £600m since promised bidding pause
raw_text:
Fujitsu has raked in an average of over £200m a year in UK taxpayer cash in the three years since its “hollow” gesture not to bid for government contracts.

The shamed supplier, whose software is at the centre of the Post Office scandal, made promises in the immediate aftermath of ITV’s dramatisation of what is often described as the widest miscarriage of justice in UK history, but what has followed has amounted to little more than PR stunts.

Nearly three years on, a promised contract bidding pause has been ineffective, Fujitsu is yet to meet its self-confessed “moral obligation” and contribute towards costs of the scandal, and the children of subpostmasters claim the IT giant is hiding from its commitments to them, behind the restorative justice programme.

In January 2024, when the scandal became wider public knowledge and entered mainstream public debate, Fujitsu was quick to show regret, and made promises to the government and victims. However, there has been a delay through caveats and small print in regard to Fujitsu’s commitments.

The company, which relies heavily on public sector work in its UK business, immediately made a commitment not to bid for public sector contracts until after the Post Office statuary public inquiry reported. But, according to figures from Tussell, since the then European boss, Paul Patterson, made the promise in January 2024, Fujitsu has won over £624m in government contracts, including the latest £24.8m Horizon extension.

At the time, the bidding pause was described as “hollow” by peer Kevan Jones, a staunch supporter of the subpostmasters in their long battle with the Post Office and Fujitsu.

Peer James Arbuthnot, who has campaigned for subpostmasters for nearly two decades, said: “£624m is just under the figure I first suggested (£700m) would be a suitable interim payment from Fujitsu. If the company had a sense of shame or honour, it would make such a payment now.”

In early 2024, Patterson also told MPs and the public that it was the supplier’s “moral obligation” to pay its share of the costs covered by taxpayers in relation to the scandal, standing in the billions of pounds today. It has gone on to delay, and has so far not paid a penny, stating that it will wait until after a public inquiry to commit a figure. This comes despite repeated calls for the global giant to pay an interim sum. The inquiry report is expected soon, as reported last week.

Read more: Post Office Horizon scandal explained: Everything you need to know

At around the same time, the Japanese supplier, through Patterson again, also made lofty promises to the children and wider families of subpostmasters affected by the scandal. But according to Katie Burrows, who chairs the Lost Chances charity, set up in March 2024 to support them, the supplier has done nothing since, and is hiding behind the restorative justice programme.

Asked what, if any, financial or other type of contribution it has made to Lost Chances, a Fujitsu spokesperson said: “We remain committed to supporting the Restorative Justice Council’s independent work, and to playing our part in the wider process of meaningful change, learning and repair.”

According to the Restorative Justice Council, which is running the Post Office scandal-related programme: “The process is strictly voluntary and independent of financial compensation schemes, focusing instead on emotional acknowledgment, truth-telling and rebuilding dignity.”

Read more: Fujitsu’s role in the Post Office scandal: Everything you need to know

Burrows told Computer Weekly: “Following our meeting with Paul Patterson in 2024, there has been absolutely nothing. Seriously, nothing.

“We had that meeting and there was talk of them making a donation to the charity, but then that’s just fallen on deaf ears,” she said. “And since then, they have just deflected to the restorative justice programme. They use it as like a barrier between us and them, and just basically said we’re dealing with restorative justice.

“I don’t know how much this programme has cost. But they just seem to want to give money to everyone else. Apart from the victims,” said Burrows.

“Reports, reports, reports. ‘We’re going to do this, we’re going to do that’. Why don’t they give the charity money so we can just help people get therapy at the very least?”

Jim Simon, CEO at the Restorative Justice Council, said: “We have engaged with Fujitsu, along with the Post Office and the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, about their participation in the restorative justice process.

“Our focus remains on delivering an independent restorative justice process that enables those affected to have their experiences heard and to engage directly with the organisations involved.”

Burrows’ mother, Elaine Hood, ran a post office branch in Allestree, Derby, from the 1980s. She was wrongfully prosecuted for theft in 2002, which resulted in a conviction that has now been overturned in the Court of Appeal.

In 2002, customers stood up for her and provided the court with statements supporting her. Legendary former Derby County and Nottingham Forest football manager Brian Clough, who was a friend of her father, also provided a statement in support of her.

summary:
Fujitsu has raked in an average of over £200m a year in UK taxpayer cash in the three years since its “hollow” gesture not to bid for government contracts.

The shamed supplier, whose software is at the centre of the Post Office scandal, made promises in the immediate aftermath of ITV’s dramatisation of what is often described as the widest miscarriage of justice in UK history, but what has followed has amounted to little more than PR stunts.

Nearly three years on, a promised contract bidding pause has been ineffective, Fujitsu is yet to meet its self-confessed “moral obligation” and contribute towards costs of the scandal, and the children of subpostmasters claim the IT giant is hiding from its commitments to them, behind the restorative justice programme.

In January 2024, when the scandal became wider public knowledge and entered mainstream public debate, Fujitsu was quick to show regret, and made promises to the government and victims. However, there has been a delay through caveats and small print in regard to Fujitsu’s commitments.

The company, which relies heavily on public sector work in its UK business, immediately made a commitment not to bid for public sector contracts until after the Post Office statuary public inquiry reported. But, according to figures from Tussell, since the then European boss, Paul Patterson, made the promise in January 2024, Fujitsu has won over £624m in government contracts, including the latest £24.8m Horizon extension.

At the time, the bidding pause was described as “hollow” by peer Kevan Jones, a staunch supporter of the subpostmasters in their long battle with the Post Office and Fujitsu.

Peer James Arbuthnot, who has campaigned for subpostmasters for nearly two decades, said: “£624m is just under the figure I first suggested (£700m) would be a suitable interim payment from Fujitsu. If the company had a sense of shame or honour, it would make such a payment now.”

In early 2024, Patterson also told MPs and the public that it was the supplier’s “moral obligation” to pay its share of the costs covered by taxpayers in relation to the scandal, standing in the billions of pounds today.

title: CFO Colette Kress leads Nvidia Q3 with GPU commitment
raw_text:
The latest quarterly results from Nvidia show continued growth as the company looks for a new chief executive after its co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down.

The graphics processor unit (GPU) chipmaker reported revenue for the third quarter of $116bn, up 20% from the previous quarter and up 103% from a year ago.

“Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice-president and chief financial officer of Nvidia.

Following the departure of Huang, analyst firm Forrester advised IT leaders to treat Nvidia’s CEO transition as a prompt to reassess concentration risk across their AI infrastructure, suppliers and investment plans.

Commenting on the quarterly results, Brian Colello, senior equity analyst at Morningstar, said: “Nvidia’s results were solid and largely in line with our expectations, which should help ease some of the concerns created by the recent leadership turmoil. Shipments have not slipped, and we remain confident that the AI infrastructure buildout is real.

“Investors will now be looking for Nvidia to reaffirm its long-term outlook and show that the business can continue executing through the leadership transition. Longer term, there are risks around policy, international sales and hyperscalers developing their own chips, but Nvidia should remain an important player as the overall market continues to grow.”

Nvidia’s results come just a few weeks after US midterm polling showed that voters in the states are dismayed with politicians who have encouraged the development of new datacentre builds. A number of states with new datacentre builds, such as Texas, have flipped from the Republicans – who backed the development – to Democrats. According to a report by BBC Verify, which quoted The Voter Poll by SSRS for AP, 56% of the voters polled said datacentres and AI were major factors in their voting decision.

When asked about the change in the political climate regarding whether to continue building out datacentres, Kress said: “Where we stand right now, there is so much demand with such the largest companies continuing to work on so many agentic solutions, new models that are also available, and that’s been our focus to assist. I’d say, even in the last week, they continued ask, ‘How are we going to receive more and more supply to help them with the demand that they have in front of them?’”

She added that demand driven by agentic AI would continue through 2027 and 2028.

Responding to a question about whether Nvidia could continue to command a premium for its GPUs as customers look at alternatives such as custom chips to accelerate AI, Kress said the company would continue to assess its pricing, as it developed “world-class” systems.

“For the long term in terms of pricing, one of the most important parts of our systems is that they are world-class and everything that we enable within those systems is so important. I think our pricing is well thought through, but that is something for the future we’ll continue to think through what that pricing might be,” said Kress.

title: Teachers anxious amid pension platform problems as January rush looms
raw_text:
Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) faces the challenge of fixing problems in the Teachers’ Pension Scheme platform before the January rush of retirees.

Thousands of teachers are expected to retire in January, but current problems with the scheme administration, which TCS recently took over, are causing concern.

In 2023, Indian IT giant TCS secured the contract to administer the Teachers’ Pension Scheme, which has about two million members. Capita had run the service for well over 20 years.

After two years’ preparation, the service transferred from Capita to TCS earlier this month. Since the switch, which arrived after a two-week blackout period to migrate accounts, members have been reporting problems.

David Fountain, a retired IT teacher who supports teachers in relation to the pension platform, set up an online survey on a dedicated Facebook page to gain feedback on the new platform.

At the time of writing, there had been 436 survey respondents. It has found that nearly 45% reported being unable to log in to the members’ area of the pension platform. Over 53% of those unable to access it said it was because the system could not find a user record for them, while 23% did not receive a verification email.

A total of 242 respondents said their nominated death beneficiary was not shown, while 29% could not see their employment history.

TCS acknowledged the issues, and said they are a “consequence of a large-scale and security-critical data migration that TCS is managing as part of a controlled service transition”.

“We understand that some Teachers’ Pension Scheme members are experiencing challenges in accessing the portal and with some of the information they may need,” it said.

The sample in the survey is very small in the context of two million members, and Fountain admitted people are more likely to visit his website if they are having problems. However, he stressed that hundreds of people are having problems and warned that come January, when a few thousand teachers are likely to retire, there could be problems.

He said about 10,000 teachers retire each year in three windows, with the main one in September, and smaller numbers in January and April.

Teachers can begin to apply six months before, and Fountain said thousands will currently be planning to retire. However, the current problems mean they may not have access to the right information to get their pensions confirmed on time, he told Computer Weekly.

Huge concern

Fountain stated that he is “incredibly concerned”.

“If you have half the people unable to log in, they can’t make an online application, they can’t see the figures that they will be basing their decisions whether they can retire on,” he told Computer Weekly. “They have to know the numbers and they can’t see them.”

Retired university lecturer Tom said he has been unable to log in to his account and is very anxious about his pension.

When trying to access his account, he was greeted with the message: “We couldn’t verify your details. Please check your information and try again, or Contact Teachers’ Pensions for assistance.”

The scheme member said: “For reasons that will be clear if you have been following the Facebook group, I have no intention of trying to contact Teachers’ Pensions.”

There are reports in the Facebook community of members spending hours on the phone trying to get help.

He said: “This whole thing has caused anxiety. First of all, I wasn’t aware that this changeover was going to happen. I don’t recall ever getting any notification of it.

“I went around the internet and finally found the Facebook page where there’s a lot of dialogue between teachers retired and expecting retirement with some not getting their payments and not being able to get through for help.” He said the page has been helpful to him.

“This whole process is continuing to be very upsetting because at my age, I am over 80, I’ve got plenty of other problems to worry about, and if the money suddenly stopped coming in, that would be very serious,” he added.

Read more about Teachers Pension scheme migration

  • Members braced as Teachers’ Pension transfer approaches.
  • Teachers’ pension transfers from Capita on eve of government’s civil service scheme decision.
  • Teachers surprised pension service not fully returned after migration blackout.

The transfer of the Teachers’ Pension Scheme to TCS was completed on 2 November, but, as Computer Weekly recently reported, to the surprise of teachers, the two-week blackout for the switchover of the scheme from Capita was not the final stage expected by members, with services still to be brought online.

Teachers had expected the migration to be complete, but there was still work to do.

TCS added: “We appreciate members deserve the best possible service, and we are working to deliver full access as quickly as we can. Our immediate priority is delivering improvements to the portal access process in line with member feedback.”

The Department for Education did not respond to Computer Weekly’s request for comment.

Fears of civil service repeat

The disastrous transfer of the Civil Service Pension Scheme over the past 12 months has fuelled anxiety, said Tom. Delays of as much as a year have left retired civil servants in financial difficulty, and some have died before receiving their pensions, which were due.

As reported by Computer Weekly last month, MPs heard in the run-up to transfer that some teachers were experiencing problems.

Alison Bennet, Liberal Democrat MP for Mid Sussex, said she had been told teachers were experiencing problems with their pensions. She asked: “Are we seeing teachers go through the same ordeal [as civil servants]?

“I received very concerning casework from teachers in my constituency who seem to be having similar or the same troubles with their pensions,” added Bennet. “The idea that the immense stress and potential financial hardship we’ve heard inflicted on civil servants has been [repeated] with teachers is appalling.”

title: The cyber threats to businesses from ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’
raw_text:
Having waited 13 years since the last full release in the series, fans of Rockstar Games’ blockbuster video game franchise, Grand Theft Auto (GTA), have been a patient bunch. That changes this week, with the anticipated launch of the sixth instalment in the series, GTA VI.

While downloads of GTA VI have already begun – spiking global network traffic, as previously reported by Computer Weekly – the game’s official release date on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S consoles is still a few hours off, with a rolling release set for midnight in your local time zone on Thursday 19 November.

Unfortunately, the launch of the hottest new gaming property in years carries with it a host of cyber concerns.

But why should video games be a cyber concern for businesses? Who is gaming on company time? Plenty of people, it turns out, and they’re not always employees slacking off.

Recent research by Claroty – a specialist in cyber physical systems protection – found significant numbers of consumer devices, including gaming consoles, running on operational technology (OT), healthcare and other enterprise networks.

In compiling its report, titled Game over for consumer tech risk in critical infrastructure, Claroty’s team analysed 45 million devices running at 30,000 sites and found more than 65,000 “non-essential” devices running adjacent to often mission-critical industrial control systems (ICS) and medical tech.

This total included 16,745 consoles on OT and healthcare networks – 95% of which were running on production networks instead of isolated guest or virtual local area networks (VLANs) – as well as media devices from the likes of Roku and Sonos.

Lifecycle management

Although in some cases – such as on children’s wards in hospitals – there may be a clear benefit to allowing such devices, consoles still lack the necessary security rigour and lifecycle management oversight required to operate safely on the same network as critical intensive care unit (ICU) kit.

Often, such devices will contain unpatched firmware and known remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, and have outdated operating systems, while their frequent communication with supplier-hosted cloud services brings unmanaged external connections.

“Finding consumer technology like Apple Watches and Nintendo Switches residing on the same networks as OT and medical equipment points directly to ongoing deficiencies in network governance and segmentation within operational settings,” said Sean Tufts, field chief technology officer at Claroty.

“[But] addressing this issue does not mean stripping smart TVs from conference rooms or banning Xbox consoles from hospitals; it requires closing off unnecessary pathways for malicious actors from causing intolerable disruptions and negatively impacting businesses across industries.”

To combat this and safeguard the resilience of critical systems, security teams should audit their connected assets, adopt more rigorous access controls and introduce network segmentation, said Claroty’s team.

In enforcing continuous asset discovery and segmentation between guest, internet of things (IoT) and core production environments, organisations can eliminate unmanaged entry points and stop threat actors from conducting lateral movement from something like an Xbox to something truly mission-critical. This guidance essentially holds true for any organisation, whether or not it is engaged in a critical sector.

Real-world threats

Cyber company Darktrace has also been on the trail of threat actors exploiting the GTA VI release. According to its cyber analyst, Gemma Stubberfield, it detected suspicious activity linked to the video game across organisations in multiple sectors.

In particular, wrote Stubberfield, the firm observed 12 of its corporate customer environments connecting to gta6demo[dot]asia, a domain known to be associated with a fake GTA VI demo package used to distribute the Vidar infostealer.

These connections were all observed in September and October 2026, and occurred in both EMEA – including the UK – and North America, with affected organisations ranging across sectors such as defence, finance, manufacturing and public affairs.

A few weeks ago, on 7 October, the Darktrace team found itself on the trail of a device making suspicious domain name system (DNS) requests for gta6-play[dot]ru, a Russian-language GTA VI site previously flagged as potentially malicious in open source intelligence (OSINT).

This site advertised a GTA VI download via a separate page containing a Windows executable packaged using the commercial InstallMate framework. Ultimately, this contained functionality designed to inspect the environment it was running in, including enumerating installed software and disks, network adaptors, MAC addresses, and running processes and window titles. It also hunted for processes associated with virtualisation, debugging and network analysis.

This is not in and of itself proof that the executable was malicious, and no malicious payload or command-and-control (C2) infrastructure was found by Darktrace, but Butterfield said it is still a useful finding since it demonstrates how a user seeking content could easily move from an unofficial gaming site to an executable that inspected their environment and, critically, checked for software commonly used by security researchers. What reason would a legitimate executable have to do that?

Educating users

So, how are the threats outlined by the Darktrace team getting through to users? It’s an easy question to answer because there is so much precedent to draw on; countless times down through the years we have witnessed cyber fraudsters and scammers latching onto high-profile events; the World Cup, Christmas and Black Friday, the General Election, the Olympic Games, all are heavily targeted.

Cyber criminals exploit human behaviour just as readily as they do vulnerabilities, and the warnings this activity draws from the industry should by now be familiar. Moreover, the once-in-a-decade release of a much-loved video game is certainly a high-profile event, said KnowBe4 senior cyber security threat researcher Lucy Gee.

“Cyber criminals are wasting no time capitalising on the excitement surrounding GTA VI,” she said. “We’ve identified a staggering 1,300% surge in gaming-related phishing emails compared with the monthly average between March and August 2026.

“In the week beginning 26 October, GTA-related scams alone accounted for 9.6% of phishing emails analysed, demonstrating just how quickly attackers are exploiting anticipation around the game’s launch.”

Read more about cyber attacks in the gaming sector

  • Bandai Namco, developer of video games including Pac-Man, Tekken and Dark Souls, has broken days of silence to confirm it has been hit by a cyber attack.
  • Video game studio Capcom says the data of up to 350,000 people was likely to have been compromised in a Ragnar Locker ransomware attack.
  • Theories that the cyber attack on a high-profile gaming studio was orchestrated by players who are disappointed in a video game are likely wide of the mark, according to analysis.

Gee said it was particularly concerning that these scams are not just targeting gamers. “Attackers are using fake employee benefits and free GTA VI pre-order offers to steal corporate credentials, with 83.2% of this targeted attack volume occurring over weekends,” she said. “They’re also using QR codes to move employees from protected work devices onto personal phones, potentially bypassing corporate security controls.”

Security teams can get out in front of this particular problem with a cyber awareness blitz. Users should be made aware of where their employers are offering genuine benefits and how to access those, and taught to verify unexpected offers through official internal channels. It might not be a bad idea to conduct a few phishing simulations at the same time.

For users, whether you are browsing the web and checking email on your phone at home, or connected to the office network, you should be wary of any contact related to GTA VI.

In particular, emails promising early access or free copies of the game, or other promotions that seem to be from official retailers, should be treated with extreme caution, particularly if they create a sense of urgency or seem too good to be true.

Chris Mawson, founder of gaming news site Power Up Gaming, shared some essential tips for those anxiously waiting for GTA VI.

  • There is no beta testing programme open to the public, and even if there was, it would not be inviting signups on the eve of release – trust that Rockstar has play-tested its new property at this point;
  • There is no official demo download – at best, any download will probably be an infostealer, and running a demo seems rather pointless so close to release, so be patient and don’t touch them;
  • There are no early access GTA VI builds or VIP programmes – and if there were, they wouldn’t be hiding behind cryptocurrency paywalls – sign up to one of these and you will probably have your digital wallet drained in short order;
  • There are no official mobile or PC versions of GTA VI – don’t be tricked into downloading malware just because you have a fear of missing out;
  • Don’t be tempted to game the system by downloading a repack version of GTA VI, which may be “sold” as enabling the game to be installed without needing a launcher – these will almost certainly be malware;
  • Protect your credentials – although the official version was largely phased out during a recent restructure, there are still plenty of Rockstar Social Club login pages in the wild, these are designed to steal official Rockstar account credentials. Always be sure you are accessing your Rockstar account through an official site by verifying the URL first, especially if you are being asked to log in to “unlock” content, which is a huge red flag;
  • Ultimately, remember that GTA VI will only be sold through official channels, and the safest way to engage with the new game is to do so through these – giveaways on YouTube or TikTok may seem tempting, but don’t engage with them.

title: UK government warned that lax AI safety undermines GDP boost
raw_text:
The Guardrails for growth: making AI safe report from the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee (BIST) has presented a case for more control over how artificial intelligence (AI) develops.

Liam Byrne MP, chair of BIST, said: “AI could expand our economy by £400bn larger in just a decade. We have world-leading expertise in AI testing but clear rules and credible safeguards are now needed.

“We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control. AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinise them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled.”

Drawing on oral witness statements from experts along with insiders from frontier model providers, the report’s authors noted that AI will only be optimised if it is trusted by individuals, businesses and public institutions.

When asked why he left his job as a researcher in the governance division of OpenAI, Daniel Kokotajlo said he lost confidence in the leadership of the business to consider AI safety as an important issue: “OpenAI, Anthropic and some of these other companies are trying to build superintelligence. For years, these companies have been saying, ‘Yes, this would be incredibly transformative. Yes, it could go really badly, but it could also go really well. That is why we need to be the ones doing it, because we are the good guys.’

“I left OpenAI because I came to believe that OpenAI, in fact, would not behave responsibly around the creation of this technology and that OpenAI was rationalising why it needed to be in the lead and build this as fast as possible. Basically, I lost confidence in the leadership,” he told BIST.

Another former OpenAI employee, Steve Adler, spoke about reluctance in the business to use the word “dangerous” when talking about AI technology, adding: “I also saw, while working at the company, the ways in which there was pressure not to speak candidly as a scientist. There was pressure not to use words such as ‘dangerous’ and to play up the benefits of artificial intelligence and not just talk about the risks in ways that I felt were distortive.”

He also told BIST that he witnessed how the company moved fast without acknowledging the gravity of the stakes.

When asked to explain why he thinks there is a 50% chance that AI will destroy society, Geoffrey Irving, chief scientist at the government’s AI Safety institute, said: “There is a broad trend. If you build machines that are, first, better than humans at a number of key skills – which are hacking, persuasion, planning and concealment – and then, potentially, eventually better than us at everything, that is a large evolutionary push.” 

He said the way out is to stop building this kind of technology.

Aengus Lynch, who collaborated with Anthropic on three research papers, told the committee that he tried to launch a third-party alignment evaluator business because he was worried that there was no infrastructure to hold AI labs to account. However, the idea failed to gain enough traction. He said embedded evaluators identify risks ahead of time and then work with the AI developer looking for evidence that the risk is being mitigated and test that the detection methods work.

“Until you have embedded evaluators, which ahead of time commit to risks they want to catch...it is very hard to take any company’s word [on AI safety]. Only the embedded evaluators have an incentive to do a good job of quantifying [AI risk],” he said.

Along with the risks presented in the witness statements, the report also warns that Chinese developers are producing increasingly open-weight models, which are easy to adopt and difficult to control once released.

“Their low cost and ease of access will likely accelerate global adoption and so AI systems developed outside the UK could become widely embedded in the economy,” the report’s authors warned.

  • Trying to separate hype from fact: The danger is not a conscious machine, but a dazzling prediction engine that moves faster than we can supervise. The real risk is that we hand over the controls too easily.
